title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
body_text: The End of AI Frontiers – Machine Learning (Theory) Skip to content Machine Learning (Theory) Machine learning and learning theory research Posted on 11/6/2026 11/7/2026 by John Langford The End of AI Frontiers In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR. In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion. We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines. In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI . On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex- Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. In a scaling-only environment of course the primary effort is on getting/making/refining data, which is quite a step away from what we were working on. Aside from the incompatible focus, there was plenty of evidence that they just did not really want us. It’s a tough situation to find yourself in. I consider the scaling-only focus to be both misdirected and not fun. It is an understandable failure mode—scaling is straightforward and it’s common for people to give up on a tradeoff between multiple competing ideals (like innovation and size) by short-sightedly adopting one in totality and dropping the other. But returns to research are real and significant. For example, the Bytedance experiments suggest a variant of the Full Bandwidth Transformer might be comparable to a model of twice the size, implying significant savings in training and inference for the same capability. Do the math—how much is it worth to halve training and inference cost given that the industry has investments approaching a trillion dollars? So I situated my folks as best I could and left. I am quite fortunate in that there are many other people in the world who are capable of seeing the value of research and innovation which is my intrinsic center of interest. Every other founding AIF leadership team member seems to have come to a similar conclusion. This does leave a question: Why not go back to MSR? I chatted with folks a bit but could not get away from two serious obstacles. The first is that I am just not comfortable being at a company where the research I do has no path to real use. I could not get innovation into use (or even seriously considered) when I was in MAI, so the prospects for success from MSR seem quite small. The second is that I’m afraid there’s a breakdown of the basic deal in MSR: do good work and good things happen. As far as I can tell we did good work and were non-consensually reorged away. Unfortunately, I would not be surprised to see that kind of thing continue to happen until MSR leadership develops a will to effectively organize to meet the moment. So AI Frontiers is over. I’m sorry to say that there will not be internships with the folks there in the coming year—I enjoyed working with interns on many occasions. And my best wishes for the folks I leave behind. It is not hard to imagine a Microsoft of the future which becomes attractive for research again if the people in control can develop a little bit more wisdom. Twitter/X thread . title: The $8 Linux Computer (2022)
What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab
body_text: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab | Bosscher before the browser paints. Runs synchronously, no defer/async. --> Skip to content Bosscher Posts Tags About Archives Search Go back What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab 7 Nov, 2026 | Edit page A while ago I bought an OpenStick on a whim for 10 dollars (including shipping!) because it seemed like such a cool novelty piece of hardware. For 10 dollars you get: 512 MB of RAM (~450 MB usable) 4x ARM Cortex-A53 CPU cores at 1 GHz 4 GB eMMC flash 150 Mbit/s Wi-Fi 4G modem and GPS Passively cooled, so 100% silent! 1 programmable LED :) Now, you might look at this hardware and think âmy watch is more powerful than thatâ, and you wouldnât necessarily be wrong, but thereâs still a lot of fun to be had with a device this size, and itâs a great gadget to get started with self-hosting. The installation process is a bit involved, but once youâre up and running it runs Debian, which brings all the classic goodies such as systemd (among other things, a scheduler and service monitoring for Linux) and Podman (lightweight containerization). For 10 USD you basically get a home server with minimal power usage and zero noise! Thereâs actually a lot of useful software that runs great on this thing. Some of my favorites are: CastSponsorSkip (5â10 MB) This is a little service that connects to any running Google Cast device and skips sponsorships (and sometimes ads). It barely uses any resources, and after a while you forget that it exists, but it does make the whole YouTube experience a lot nicer! CastSponsorSkip AdGuard Home - my own fork (40 MB) AdGuard Home blocks bad domains at the DNS level: spyware, malware, and so on. These days devices have a tendency to spy on you. Smart TVs run content recognition continuously, washing machines scan your network, and your coffee maker might be spying on you. A DNS blocker cannot block all bad requests (youâll need a proper firewall for that), but it sure can block a whole lot. After adding a few blocklists, 60% of my queries are now blocked. Most seem harmless, but Iâm pretty sure that some arenât. Iâm running my own fork, which can handle large blocklists in an efficient manner, but you probably shouldnât run binaries provided by random strangers, so Iâve also included the link to the official version below (which is totally fine if you limit yourself to smaller blocklists). AdGuard Home Next-Gen - 40 MB (independent of the size of the blocklist) AdGuard Home - 40 MB (with a small (200k) blocklist) Zeroclaw (64 MB) Zeroclaw is an AI agent harness. It supports 30 channels (Telegram, email, WhatsApp, etc.), has sensible security defaults, a nice web UI, and integrations with all the major LLM providers. I ran OpenClaw for a while on my Kubernetes cluster, but it mostly caused a lot of frustration: it worked, but it used 1 GB+ of memory, broke with every update, and they kept changing functionality in ways that broke my existing workflows. Zeroclaw feels like a breath of fresh air. It uses ~3 MB RSS when idle, covers all the functionality that I need, and the security defaults are sensible and easy enough to disable. The next version will (hopefully!) have rich message support for Telegram, implemented by yours truly. The PR can be tracked here! Iâve given Zeroclaw access to the OpenStick (but nothing beyond that). Effectively itâs a root shell, but given that the blast radius is limited, I figured it would be acceptable. I mostly use this to monitor the OpenStick, with questions such as âanything in the logs that requires my attention?â or âhow is the disk space?â. The biggest advantage is that it communicates through Telegram, so if Iâm in the mountains with limited signal, I can still ask it how my little server is doing :) I looked at alternatives such as Picoclaw and Nullclaw, and no doubt theyâre good as well. However, Zeroclaw seemed to have the best documentation and the most active community, so I went with that :) GitHub Zeroclaw Documentation Cloudflare Tunnel (~8-20 MB) Cloudflared makes it possible to expose all these services securely to the big, bad internet, for free, without exposing any ports. The downside might be that the NSA might be able to read everything you do, but for a homelab I consider that to be an acceptable trade-off. Cloudflare Tunnel Beszel (20 MB) Beszel shows a pretty graph of memory, CPU usage, and so on, and alerts you if something looks suspicious, all while using very little memory. I ran Grafana and the whole stack on my Kubernetes cluster for a while, and itâs powerful, but not extremely user friendly, and it felt like overkill. Beszel is a really awesome solution: it looks pretty and requires ~20 MB, 10 MB for the agent and 10 MB for the server. It has built-in alerting for a whole bunch of protocols, and I let it send messages to Telegram when something requires my attention. GitHub Beszel Dozzle Dozzle is a pretty interface for managing Podman containers. It has a large overlap with Beszel, so if I ever need to save 10 or 20 MB, Iâll get rid of one of them. Dozzle has a way better interface for checking Podman logs, but it doesnât offer the same level of stats as Beszel does. GitHub Dozzle Gatus (10 MB) Beszel monitors your server(s). Gatus monitors your services. In other words, if you would like to get a notification when your webserver or database has crashed, youâll want Gatus. It also creates a really pretty web interface! GitHub Gatus - 10 MB Fusion RSS (22 MB) RIP Google Reader . I tried Feedly for a while, but 7 USD for the Pro version was just a little bit more than I felt comfortable with. Besides, why pay when you can have hours of fun setting up your own alternative? I tried a whole bunch of RSS readers and eventually settled on Fusion. It does all I need, looks good, feels responsive, and uses 22 MB of RAM. GitHub Fusion - 22 MB Shiori (~10â20 MB) Browser bookmarks are great, however a lot of my older bookmarks have stopped working because the sites disappeared, the URLs changed, or for a myriad of other reasons. Shiori fixes this by offering a great bookmark manager that also automatically archives the website. It does so in ~10 MB. You can expect some spikes when archiving, but nothing that our mighty OpenStick cannot handle! Shiori - 10 MB Diun (9 MB) Just a little service that sends a message to my Telegram whenever one of my containers has an update available. Diun - 9 MB Edit page Back to top OpenStick Linux Zeroclaw Beszel Gatus Fusion RSS Adguard Home Ad blocking Shiori Share this post: Share this post on X Share this post via email Bosscher on Github Copyright © 2026  |  All rights reserved.

title: Person of Interest
body_text: Person of Interest – Wilson Tovar (krthr) Wilson Tovar (krthr) home • blog • poesía • photography • say hi 👋 Person of Interest 07 Nov, 2026 A few days ago, I started watching Person of Interest, and I haven’t been able to stop. Aside from the fact that the show feels even more relevant today than it did 15 years ago, when it first aired, it’s brought back so many memories of the early 2010s, when I first started getting into tech and developing an interest in computers. It’s reminded me of all the forums and online communities I used to be part of as a teenager, the whole SOPA and PIPA controversy, the shutdown of Megaupload, and just what the Internet was like back then. I also find it pretty crazy and, frankly, a little sad to think that something like the Machine, which seemed like pure science fiction at the time, isn't all that far from our reality today. But beyond all that, watching it has made me incredibly nostalgic, and considering it’s already 15 years old, I think it’s aged remarkably well. Hace unos días empecé a ver Person of Interest y no he podido parar. Más allá de que la serie se siente incluso más actual que hace 15 años, cuando se estrenó, me ha hecho recordar mucho los primeros años de la década de 2010, que fue cuando empecé a meterme en el mundillo informático y a interesarme por los computadores. Me ha traído muchos recuerdos de los foros y las comunidades online en las que participaba siendo adolescente, de todo el rollo de SOPA y PIPA, del cierre de Megaupload y, en general, de cómo era Internet en aquella época. También me parece muy loco y, siendo franco, un poco triste pensar que algo como la Máquina, que en aquel entonces parecía sacado de la ciencia ficción, hoy no esté tan lejos de nuestra realidad. Pero, más allá de eso, verla me ha despertado mucha nostalgia y, teniendo en cuenta que ya tiene 15 años, me parece que ha envejecido bastante bien —- Discussion here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50412318#50413753 #tech   Subscribe to my blog via email or RSS feed . title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
body_text: We Know 15,579 Websites Are Infected. How Do We Tell Them? Home Speaking Training Media Contact Sponsor 🌙 Subscribe Sponsored by:   Report URI - SuperPixel: a card skimmer hiding inside 100+ shops' own copy of jQuery. Would you have spotted it? Threat Intelligence We Know 15,579 Websites Are Infected. How Do We Tell Them? Scott Helme Security researcher, entrepreneur and international speaker who specialises in web technologies. More posts by Scott Helme. Scott Helme 6 Nov 2026 • 5 min read We've identified 15,579 websites that are currently infected with malicious JavaScript and between them, we conservatively estimate that they receive more than 135 million visits every month. We know they're infected, and we have the evidence to back that up, but there's a problem: how on Earth do we tell them all? As our Threat Intelligence capabilities at Report URI have grown, identifying compromised websites has become increasingly efficient. Unfortunately, responsible disclosure hasn't kept pace, and we're now finding infections considerably faster than we could ever hope to notify the affected organisations. I genuinely don't know how to solve this problem, so I'm asking for help. What attacks we're finding At the core of it, we're finding websites that are running JavaScript that they should absolutely not be running! For some examples of how nasty this can be: Credit card skimmers - often known as ' Magecart ', they target payment pages and skim full card details to send them to the attacker. ClickFix attacks - designed to trick users into completing a "prove you're human" challenge and instead installing malware on their device. Device exploitation - loading malware to compromise specific versions of iOS and install spyware, like DarkSword or Coruna . Redirects - these can send the visitor anywhere, including fake login pages to phish details, device security 'warnings', scams, and much more. All of these are bad scenarios for the innocent visitor, and attackers change their payloads depending on their objective. How these sites are compromised There are many ways an attacker can get malicious JS onto a site, but here are the main categories that we group the initial vectors into from what we're seeing: Direct compromise - typically a WordPress vulnerability or similar, the site's own JS files are modified to include the malicious JS. Supply chain - a third-party script file that a site loads is infected with malware, and is then loaded on to the site, exposing all visitors. XSS - good old traditional XSS, a vulnerability in the site itself that allows JS to be injected. DeadTag - a threat group we named recently, buying expired domains that sites still load JS from, reviving them, and serving malware. Unfortunately, there are a lot of different ways that this can go wrong, as we're seeing. The scale of the problem Right now, we have 15,579 unique sites that are infected with one of the malicious JS attacks listed above. Those are the sites where there is no doubt in our mind, and the list of sites where we have some suspicion but haven't got to 100% confidence is thousands more. Take September as an example, because we haven't quite finished processing everything from October yet, and this is the tally for new sites that we identified as being infected: These are the sites that, as of today, are still infected. We remove sites once they clear their own infection as we have no concern about trying to notify them, so there were more than this. In terms of traffic volumes, it's quite surprising how quickly this adds up. None of the sites in the list are global leaders, but we do have a huge presence of regional leaders. For example, if we look at .fr , .es and .de sites, some of them are really highly ranked sites in those countries, but they barely crack the Top 1 Million globally. Being a top site in France still gets you quite a hefty amount of traffic it turns out. Using various sources of data, and being ultra-conservative with our estimates, our list of currently infected sites is comfortably receiving a combined 135 million visits a month. That's a lot of exposure. So, what do we do? We continue to reach out directly to those sites that we identify as particularly high impact and try to notify them, though this is happening on an admittedly small scale. The process of responsible disclosure consumes a lot of resources, use of security.txt is low, and the vast majority of our emails and messages go unanswered. It's simply not possible for us to scale this up. As these are sites we're crawling and identifying ourselves, we have no contact information like we would for a customer. So, as things currently stand, that's where we are, and I'd like to hear suggestions on what we can do. If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would. If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details. Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you. We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action. Update: 6th Nov 2026 21:36 UTC A lot of questions have been raised across various social channels and especially the HN thread , so I thought I'd answer them in one central place: Why hasn't the list of sites been published? There are a few reasons: I didn't want this to be a 'name and shame' as the sites on that list are, after all, victims of attacks. Someone broke into their site, and the owners probably have no idea. If the list is widely disseminated and absorbed into blocklists, trying to get your domain of those lists afterwards is close to impossible. For a small business, that could be devastating. Many of these websites were likely infected because of an existing vulnerability that was exploited in something like WordPress, Magento or similar. Handing out a list of viable targets does not seem like a good idea. Why not use the WHOIS contacts? Since GDPR back in 2018, I've found that data to be mostly useless. What you get is either nothing, a registrar web form, or a relay address such as the Namecheap or GoDaddy privacy mailboxes. Why not contact the hosting providers? Because so many of these sites are behind a CDN provider or other proxy service, so the IP resolution doesn't give any indication of who the hosting provider is to contact them. Why not just send an email to every website? I could probably try to automate that, but to what email address? I'd have to hit a selection of common ones, info@, support@, abuse@, maybe others? There are also close to 16,000 of them, have you ever tried to send 16,000 emails? The manually curated emails have almost no response rate so a spammy mailshot seems unlikely to help, and could also trash my email reputation! title: Apple’s grey list: Words and phrases your iPhone won’t help you spell
body_text: Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you | Apple | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 1 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters View image in fullscreen The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters Apple Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows Aisha Down Global technology reporter Fri 6 Nov 2026 11.12 EST Last modified on Fri 6 Nov 2026 11.55 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney. But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word. New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text. So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out. Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”. The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system. The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”. But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”. In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”. The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works. The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly. Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices Read more This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect , which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes. Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year. This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied. Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning. title: Libghostty 1.0
body_text: Libghostty 1.0 – Mitchell Hashimoto Mitchell Hashimoto About Writing Misc Mitchell Hashimoto Libghostty 1.0 November 6, 2026 libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming . At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means. 1 Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had . I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm , the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty . Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt . Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux , have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. 2 ABI Stability 1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it. Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and enduring C library is ABI stability. So from the start, I took inspiration from C libraries I enjoyed working with and designed the API to have a strong, stable ABI that allows for future additions. Every object is an opaque handle. The hundreds of values you might read or write go through a small set of enum-keyed getters and setters, so we can add new values easily without introducing a new symbol. Programs with newer headers linked against an older libghostty get GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED results instead of crashes or undefined behavior. The few non-opaque structs we have carry their size so that fields can be appended later, or contain reserved padding. Enums are pinned to int on every compiler, as much as the C standard allows. Our CI enforces our ABI policy. Every change is checked with libabigail against a committed baseline on Linux, and against golden type manifests on macOS and WebAssembly. On ELF platforms, every exported symbol is also versioned, so the dynamic loader refuses to load a mismatched library by name rather than failing in some mysterious way later. Packaging In addition to ABI stability, the 1.0 release brings along the proper build tooling, tarballs, dependency licensing manifests, documentation, and more to enable every major operating system and distribution to package libghostty-vt through standard official tooling. Libghostty has its own release cycle, separate from Ghostty the application. And it has its own tarballs with only the files and dependencies libghostty needs, resulting in smaller sizes and simpler licensing verification and compatibility. Each release publishes a signed source tarball along with a companion dependencies tarball containing every Zig package in Zig's own cache layout, so a distribution can build the library completely offline. The build installs the shared and static libraries with a proper SONAME, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config, and it honors --prefix , DESTDIR , and lib64 . Debug info is kept by default so distros can split it out. All of this is documented in PACKAGING-LIBGHOSTTY.md , which ships with the tarball. Dependencies and Licensing libghostty-vt is MIT licensed. At runtime it needs nothing beyond libc, and it can be built fully freestanding if you don't want that either. 3 The library compiles in a small number of permissively licensed dependencies: simdutf and Google Highway for SIMD, a compact Unicode table for grapheme data, and Wuffs for image decoding in the Kitty graphics protocol. Both simdutf and Highway are built without libc++ , so there is no C++ standard library dependency. There is no copyleft code anywhere in the dependency tree. Every dependency is listed in a machine-readable manifest with its version, SPDX license, and hash, specifically so distros can fill in their bundled-library metadata more easily. If a distro would rather dynamically link the system simdutf or Highway, there's a build flag for that. Portability libghostty-vt is highly portable. The table below lists all the platforms and architectures that we build and test (full unit tests plus running all examples) in CI: Platform Architectures Linux (glibc, musl) x86_64 , aarch64 macOS 13+ x86_64 , aarch64 iOS 13+ aarch64 FreeBSD x86_64 , aarch64 Windows x86_64 Android aarch64 , x86_64 , arm WebAssembly wasm32 (freestanding) There is a second set of platforms we build in CI but do not run tests for. These systems all have known users; we just haven't set up the machinery for automated testing: Platform Architectures Bare metal riscv32 , thumb WebAssembly (WASI) wasm32 Windows arm64 illumos x86_64 32-bit x86 x86 Each of the tested platforms gets the artifacts it expects: Linux and FreeBSD get a shared library with a proper SONAME and versioned symbols, a static library, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config. macOS and iOS get a dylib with an @rpath install name and compatibility version, plus an XCFramework covering macOS, iOS, and the iOS simulator that drops straight into Xcode or Swift Package Manager. Windows gets a DLL with a .pdb , an import library, and a static library. The library is built with the GNU ABI, but MSVC programs link against it through the import library and CI verifies this. Android gets a shared library built against the NDK with 16 KB page size support, as required by Android 15+. WebAssembly ships in two flavors, one optimized for speed and one for size, and the small one is under a megabyte with every feature enabled. If you only need a read-only viewer, subsystems like input encoding, search, selection, and Kitty graphics can be compiled out with a build flag, which roughly halves the module. Every function stays exported and simply returns GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED so your code doesn't have to change. 4 Portability isn't just about the ability to build and run. It's also about resource usage and being able to work in a wide variety of resource environments. For resource usage, the library creates no threads, allocates only through an allocator you can customize, and uses minimal compute and memory. I've run 10,000 active terminals, each with a live shell producing output, on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. In this test, I had to use dash because bash used far more RAM than libghostty-vt and wouldn't fit into the 8 GB budget. What's Next Libghostty 1.0 is a major milestone. You can now create a terminal in ~1,500 lines of C that has more features and better performance than just about any terminal that existed in 2025, and most today in 2026. 5 And thanks to the rich ecosystem of language bindings, you can do this in every major programming language. You get this for free. For almost no effort. You can just do it. libghostty-vt is a generalized library, so we will focus on stability while implementing as many terminal protocols as exist (giving options to enable/disable them, of course) so that embedders have the luxury of choice. Every bug any libghostty-vt embedder reports makes everyone else in the ecosystem better. Every feature we ship in libghostty-vt becomes available to everyone quickly and safely. Terminals can move faster with less fragmentation. Thank you to everyone who contributed to the library, wrote bindings, filed bugs, and shipped something on top of it while the API was still experimental. As with all open source, this was the work of a large community. Docs, examples, and downloads are at lib.ghostty.org . Boo. 👻 Footnotes As usual, I hate that I have to do this for every post, but I want to note this post was completely hand-written with no AI assistance. ↩ The numbers are rough because most consumers don't report usage, but JetBrains alone reports 12.5 million recurring active users , and that's before counting everything else on the list. ↩ In the original post I wrote "not even libc!" The default build does link libc, because the SIMD paths use it and the default allocator is malloc . Turn off SIMD and the library is freestanding, which is how it runs on bare-metal RISC-V and ARM targets. ↩ The feature flags aren't WASM-specific; they work on every target. They're likely useful for things like embedded devices too. ↩ "Features" here means the set of terminal protocols and sequences understood, and "performance" means parsing throughput and memory usage, since those are the parts libghostty-vt provides. ↩ November 6, 2026 © 2026 Mitchell Hashimoto. mail twitter Twitter icon mastodon github GitHub icon linkedin LinkedIn icon

Windows 10 has 11 months left, and… Microsoft killed Windows 10 to push Windows 11, but Windows sales… Microsoft extended Windows 10, but Nvidia just made the extension meaningless… Microsoft is limiting Microsoft 365 & OneDrive on Windows 10 to… Privacy Policy Contact Us About us Select Theme: System Light Dim Dark Trending: Remove Recall AI New Start menu Windows 11 25H2 New Windows 11 ISO Windows 11 24H2 Windows 11 AI requirements Restore WordPad Home Windows 11 Windows 11 Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why: no “Starting” screen and 70% less RAM, even with two accounts signed in By Abhijith M B - November 6, 2026 0 Discord’s current Electron client and its new Rust client launching side by side on two Lenovo ThinkPads running Windows 11 Discord’s new Rust client had its friends list loaded before the current Electron app could get past its loading screen, in a 15-second clip that we found on the X account of Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy . The video had 2.3 million views at the time of writing, and Discord employees have confirmed that both apps were launched from a cold start. Vishnevskiy also revealed that the 290.2MB RAM usage on the Task Manager of the new client, which shows up as Discord Phoenix, came with two accounts signed in at once, which justifies the already efficient RAM usage. Discord Rust for Windows 11 Discord’s Rust client opens before the Electron app finishes loading “The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time,” Vishnevskiy wrote on X , and Discord’s official account also shared the clip with the current client on the left and the Rust rebuild on the right. https://www.windowslatest.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Electron-Discord-vs-Rust-Discord-where-the-new-client-opens-must-faster-than-the-old-one.mp4 We went through the video frame by frame. What’s impressive is that the current client is opened first and shows a blank dark window for about three seconds, followed by a tip that reads “In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app.” Funnily enough, the Electron app still carries a browser engine today. The new client is double-clicked roughly a second and a half later, yet its window fades in within a second. When the old app reaches its interface, about five seconds after launch, the Rust version already has the friends list loaded, while the Electron client briefly says “There are no friends online at this time.” Discord Windows app. Credit: Windows Latest Of course, people on X asked if the new app simply popped out of the system tray. “Both are cold starts, it’s really that fast. We’ve been using it internally now for a while and the first time I tried it I thought I’d forgot to close it when I opened it fresh,” replied Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord. Travis, who works on socials and community at Discord and filmed the clip, added that a tray launch would mean “the friends list would have already been loaded!” Vishnevskiy thanked him for “finding these janky old laptops,” which are ThinkPads with a Copilot key, so 2024 or newer, which I wouldn’t dare call janky or old. They’re beautiful machines! The new Discord app skips the “Starting” screen and updates in the background As you’d already know, the current app usually checks for updates and shows a “Starting” screen when you open it, which one person on X said “takes like 5-10s every time.” Asked why the new client skips it, coral said, “It bootstraps so fast + is a new architecture so we don’t need that modal at all. We auto-update in the background.” Discord starting animation. Credit: Windows Latest Discord isn’t handing updates to the Microsoft Store or Windows’ Update Orchestration Platform either, as Coral said “We do not at this moment” when asked. Discord’s Rust client uses about 70% less RAM with two accounts signed in When one reply called 290MB “still vile” for a chat app, Vishnevskiy said, “Those 4k avatar decorations gotta render somewhere ;) but joking aside this client is actually running 2 accounts concurrently which is supported in new client.” Today’s Account Switcher lets you add up to five accounts and swap between them. Asked if the new client could keep work and personal accounts running “without needing to tear down the client in between,” Vishnevskiy replied “Yup.” Again, impressive and exciting. Discord idle RAM usage. Credit: Windows Latest For comparison, a Discord employee said in December 2025 that normal usage is under 1GB, while the company tested auto-restarting the app at 4GB . So, 290.2MB is about 70% below the 1GB mark, and on our PCs, the Electron app usually idles at 1-2GB. To be clear, it’s a snapshot from an early build, and Discord hasn’t published a like-for-like benchmark of both clients, but we’ll be doing that test when we get hands-on with the Rust version. Discord did try to fix Electron from the inside. Its September patch notes say the Electron 42 upgrade cut median CPU usage by about 17%, but “at the cost of a smaller regression to p50 memory usage (~4%).” Even the Game Mode toggle it tested later doesn’t mention RAM. Discord is replacing Electron with GPUI, not Tauri Electron inherits its multi-process architecture from Chromium , so every Electron app comes with its own browser engine, with a main process and a renderer process for each window. Tauri, which many guessed Discord would pick, uses Rust for app logic but builds the interface in HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside the system’s webview , which is WebView2 on Windows. Discord went with GPUI , “A fast, hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework for Rust” from the makers of the Zed code editor. GPUI draws the interface on the GPU without any HTML, and Rust, which Discord has used since 2018, manages memory without a garbage collector. Technology What it is Role in Discord Rust Programming language New client and shared app code GPUI Rust UI framework from Zed Draws the new desktop app Electron Chromium and Node.js runtime Current desktop app, being removed Tauri Rust framework using the system webview Not used React Native Mobile app framework Current mobile apps, being removed   Why not WinUI, you ask? (At least, I thought of it). Discord hasn’t mentioned it, and it was unlikely to, as Microsoft’s native framework only runs on Windows, while GPUI already powers Zed on Windows, macOS and Linux. Discord has its own patches on top of GPUI, and Vishnevskiy said “we will see what we can upstream if relevant to the community.” Web tech stays where it makes sense, as YouTube embeds and Activities will use the system webview. “We use the native webview similar to Tauri,” Vishnevskiy said about Activities. Discord’s mobile apps drop React Native, and the web app moves to WebAssembly Phones keep native interfaces but will share app code with desktop through Rust. On React Native, Vishnevskiy explained, “Since the beginning the iOS app started as React native, Android was ported to React Native couple years ago to achieve parity as it was always lagging in features.” The browser version will keep rendering HTML, but “logic will be WASM instead of JS.” WebAssembly (WASM) lets code written in languages like Rust run inside a browser, so the web app can share the Rust code too. As for the look, whether you like it or not, “The app looks and works identically to the current one,” Vishnevskiy said. Discord’s Rust client goes into private testing soon If you can’t to try it out, Discord marketing director Ryan K. Rigney said, “Going into private testing soon. Gonna take our time to make sure it’s stable and secure first. Won’t be long, tho.” I would rather wait for them to iron out any bugs. Mark Smith , Discord’s VP of Engineering, added that “accessibility and security are just as important to us as performance,” and Coral confirmed the new client keeps your login token in the system keyring, which is Credential Manager on Windows 10 and 11. Of course, Discord is not just doing all this work for Windows. When asked if it works on Linux, Rigney replied, “Yes,” and Coral said, “a lot of people run Mac internally!” Discord hasn’t announced a public release date yet. Discord just made WhatsApp and Teams look worse on Windows 11 Electron made it easier for Discord to ship one desktop app on Windows, macOS, and Linux for a decade. But Discord has now shown that a chat app with millions of users can drop the bundled browser without a redesign. WhatsApp, Teams and Discord combined using 1.5GB RAM while being idle. Credit: Windows Latest As for the owners of the biggest messaging platforms for regular users and enterprises, Meta and Microsoft are running out of excuses. WhatsApp went from a native app that idled under 100MB to a WebView2 wrapper using up to 1.2GB , and I uninstalled it. Microsoft Teams also uses WebView2, took up 963MB doing nothing in our tests , and it doesn’t look like Redmond cares enough to go native, despite pushing WinUI. Ironically, AI got us here. Data centers soaked up DRAM supply, prices shot up, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri now says “memory is top of mind for us right now in the industry” as Microsoft trims Windows 11’s RAM usage . Apps that kept asking for more RAM are finally going on a diet, and we’ve come full circle. Are you waiting to try the Rust-based Discord when it rolls out? Support original journalism. Edit the post and re-run bin/build.py. --> Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph — Eighth Rank Skip to content the Eighth Rank Write-up Opening Played by the Bishop (Dario Pasquini) + the Knight (Michał Bazyli) 2026-10-28 Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph Every Mac since macOS 13 (allegedly) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph. The position A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3 , emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1 ; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. What is lost is someone else. 3r1rk1/pp2qppp/8/3p1b2/8/1NQ1P1B1/PP2nPPP/2R2RK1 w - - 1 19 Finding Target Apple Intelligence / Personal Knowledge Graph Affected macOS Class Privacy Personalized AI What if we told you that every Mac ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe us? Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page ( man 8 knowledgeconstructiond ), and this is all you get: man 8 knowledgeconstructiond macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83 NAME knowledgeconstructiond – A daemon that analyzes content on the device to build a general purpose knowledge graph. DESCRIPTION knowledgeconstructiond analyzes the content on this device to help build a knowledge graph representing the device and the user. It works together with intelligenceplatformd, performing some of the heavy processing tasks, to generate the knowledge graph. Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. Also, we personally ran into it in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform ; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work . I mean, if forensics folks know about this, we don't see why you should not... But we go a bit deeper. This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing). To this end, we open-source a local dashboard ( iKnow ) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac. Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: understand how attackers might exploit it. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM). We stress that this goes beyond the specific Apple personal knowledge graph, but it generally applies to any such personalized ML / assistant systems (Muse, Dot, etc.) What's in the personal knowledge graph? The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform , a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access. Likely, the most interesting is graph.db . It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity (a person, an app, an event); the object is either a plain value (a name, a handle, a date) or another entity, which is where the graph gets its edges. The predicate is the interesting part: it says what kind of relationship the system believes holds between the two. an edge, and the rows it is stored as (Me) the owner of this Mac 9100000000007919 PS500 employer CS165 employment relationship type PS45 member of Halden Labs an organization 9100000000013724 STABLE_GRAPH · THE SAME EDGE, AS THE TWO ROWS IT IS subject predicate relationshipId relationshipPredicate object 9100000000007919 PS500 4412 PS1 CS165 9100000000007919 PS500 4412 PS45 9100000000013724 every row also carries confidence, sources, sourceDuplicates and timestamp One edge of the graph (synthetic data): a person and the organization the store holds as their employer. PS500 is the id predicate.json gives employer , and its range is not an organization but a relationship type — so one edge is two rows sharing a relationshipId , one naming the kind of relationship and one pointing at the other entity. The forty-six relationship type classes in the table below exist to carry exactly that, which is what lets an edge hold a confidence of its own and be retracted later. Most of what the two daemons do is populate those predicates, and the tables kept beside them, from everything the OS will let them read. Into the graph go Contacts; Photos (faces); Calendar (titles and attendees); Family Sharing (including the age of every member); the Medical ID emergency contact in Health; events and contacts Siri Suggestions finds in Mail and Messages; people donated by apps through App Intents; and installed apps. Beside it, in tables of their own, sit who appears with whom in your photos; the communication log (who, when, which app, which direction; no content), which also pulls from your other devices; location and movement; and a long tail of device signals (screen locked, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, charging, ambient light, and a stream named ContextualUnderstanding.PhysicalSocial whose record format lists people by name, phone and email, each with a start and an end time; it reads like a log of who was physically around you, though we never saw it filled in). The first column is the id as graph.db stores it; the last says how a value gets there: copied from a source, joined from another record, derived by a rule, shipped by Apple as world knowledge, or produced by a model (in bold). Seven we could not establish, and the table says so rather than guessing. The ids and labels are Apple's; the plain-language readings are ours. How it is inferred The methods run the whole range. Most of the vocabulary is filled by plain copying (a name from Contacts, an attendee from Calendar) and rules over the copies; the interesting rows come from models: a pair of XGBoost classifiers decides who is family from 144 mostly behavioral features, two embedding models are one of ten signals the system uses to decide when two records are the same person, twelve analyzers in Photos score partner, parent, child, coworker and friend from who appears in your pictures with you, on which trips and holidays, and Apple's on-device LLM reads your messages to put a name and a relationship on a face (if Apple Intelligence is active). Whatever the method, every row lands in the graph with a confidence attached, a number between 0 and 1. The family scores live apart. Two CoreML models ship next to the ontology, EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc and EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends.mlmodelc : binary XGBoost classifiers that take 144 features and return a class and a probability over it. Their scores do not go into the triple store but into a table of their own ( entityTagging.db , one row per person, seventeen relationship columns from family to mother to coworker , recomputed every day), which is what the iKnow scorecard further down reads. Only two of those seventeen columns have a shipped model behind them; what fills the other fifteen, and how any of these probabilities would become a confidence in the graph, we could not trace. The feature names are in each model's metadata.json , in plain text. They are the clearest statement of what this system is that we have found anywhere. Sixteen of the 144: sixteen of the 144 features in metadata.json # Feature Group 5 sameLastName identity 7 photosPersonAge identity 15 nicknameContainsEmoji identity 16 sharesHomeAddress identity 18 photosAgeDifferenceCategory identity 19 iCloudFamilyMember identity 20 personOverallPopularity communication 28 personPopularityGivenSunday communication 46 personPopularityGivenNight communication 47 personPopularityGivenHome communication 57 top1PersonInteractionMechanism communication 60 photosPersonOverallPopularity photos 85 photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenMorning photos 118 photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight photos 123 photosPersonPopularityGivenHome photos 132 photosPersonPopularityGivenWeekend photos Sixteen of the 144 inputs EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc reads, numbered by their place in its metadata.json : the six this post names, and ten that show how the rest are cut (overall, by day, by time of day, by place). EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends reads the same 144 in the same order, and every one is a number. The groups are the schema's own three blocks: twenty on who the person is, forty on when and how you communicate with them, eighty-four on the photographs you both appear in. Two of the twenty, photosPersonAge and photosAgeDifferenceCategory , are read from Photos too. The names are Apple's; the group labels are ours. The identity group is the tidy story: same surname, same home address, an iCloud Family flag — and it is the small half. The bulk of the model is the other two: whom you message and who appears in your photographs, conditioned on the day of the week and the time of day, and then on both at once. photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight is a shipped feature name in a shipped classifier whose job is deciding whether someone is family. Deleting something does not delete it everywhere. The live graph forgets. Delete a contact and nothing re-derives them; the next run replaces the table wholesale. But the store keeps a second table, expired_stable_graph , beside the live one. The retracted row moves there and keeps its confidence and its sources. How long it stays there is not clear from what we could see. It seems to go after about 48 hours (the store keeps a prune watermark, and a recent snapshot of the table reached back no further than that); but on our own Mac, we could still read very old records in it. And a conclusion can outlive the evidence for it. On our Mac, the scorecard still scored two people the graph had dropped the day before, both of them known to it only from a calendar invitation. Look into your own data Is any of this sensitive? We'll leave that to you, since "sensitive" means different things to different people (though we think you have plenty to choose from here). However, the thing is, none of it lives in isolation.
