title: Asahi Linux Progress Linux 7.3
body_text: Progress Report: Linux 7.3 - Asahi Linux About Community Contribute Governance Documentation GitHub Blog Merch Donate / Blog / Progress Report: Linux 7.3 Progress Report: Linux 7.3 Previous Well here we are again. Linux 7.3 is out and it’s been an eventful few months, so let’s get stuck in to another Asahi Linux progress report! Upstreaming continues As always, upstreaming work continues to progress. Aside from the usual patches for low-level SoC blocks, two major drivers made it on to the list this cycle: macaudio and avd. Getting macaudio ready for submission has been a challenge. The audio subsystem on Apple Silicon devices is rather special, and required quite a number of core ALSA changes to properly support it. Apple also uses special variants of speaker and headset amplifiers that were already supported upstream, and these drivers also needed some pretty significant modifications. We have previously discussed a lot of this work at length, and we are finally in a position where we can submit the main driver for review. The driver and Devicetree changes represent a hefty chunk of our total patchset, about 3100 lines. AVD is a whole different beast. The AVD driver has spent barely 3 months in our downstream tree and is already on the list. This is our shortest turnaround time yet for a major SoC component and bodes well for a transition to upstream-first development some time in the future. This is fantastic news, as the AVD driver and related Devicetree changes are around 13000 lines of code. Also making an appearance on the list this cycle are initial Devicetrees not only for M4 Pro and Max devices but also M5 thanks to Yureka’s tireless efforts. As usual these initial Devicetrees are barebones and only sufficient to boot the SoC to a TTY, however work is progressing on further enablement. Watch this space! We have also begun shifting to an upstream-first approach where practical. Changes to the TI USB-PD and SPMI drivers required for new devices, as well as initial support for Thunderbolt, were all developed upstream-first. We are so thrilled to see our focus on upstreaming starting to pay off! M3 goes GA Last time, we announced initial support for M3 series machines via the EXPERT flag on the Asahi installer. We are pleased to announce that we received almost no issues from early adopters, so M3 support is now generally available without the EXPERT flag! We have also made a number of improvements to M3 support, most notably enabling DCP. On top of performance and battery life improvements, this also allows us to enable sleep on M3 series devices and make the area around the notch useable on the MacBooks! Keep an eye out for m1n1 and kernel updates in the coming days. Crowded House Last time, we teased support for virtualising SPTM-enabled versions of macOS in m1n1, which enables reverse engineering on M4 series machines. M5 presents a new challenge, as the versions of macOS which support it all require the use of Exclaves. Exclaves are small applications running in an isolated environment controlled by the Secure Kernel. On M5 series SoCs and above, macOS uses them for sensitive tasks such as drawing the “camera in use” indicator to the screen. XNU communicates with the Secure Kernel and its Exclaves via SPTM, using yet another IPC protocol called Tightbeam. Much as with SPTM, XNU will panic if it cannot find the running Exclaves. This is all starting to look very similar in concept to Arm’s own TrustZone feature. While some Exclaves can be bypassed by changing some settings on the command line, we predict that this will not always be the case. As such, Sven started looking at how we could fit all of this in to m1n1. First line of investigation, try putting the Secure Kernel and Exclave userspace in another VM next to SPTM and macOS. Oh, that worked , and we’re now up to spawning three VMs in EL1 under m1n1! Maybe we can start selling m1n1 to companies fleeing VMWare… With that, we can now virtualise and reverse engineer macOS on both M4 and M5 series machines. Hello Triangle(s)! While M3 support is now mostly at feature parity with M1 and M2, the very obvious exception to this is the GPU. Apple’s GPU team seems to follow a tick-tock model, and the M3’s GPU was a very significant departure from the models found on M1 and M2 SoCs. We mentioned quite some time ago that the M3 GPU was being reverse engineered by a new group of contributors, however not much has been said since. At XDC this year, Alyssa Millburn , Anna Maniscalco and TellowKrinkle gave a talk on their progress reverse engineering the M3 GPU. Work has progressed far enough for m1n1 to successfully initialise the GPU and for the team to draw a triangle! Fans of the “Think Different” sections of these progress reports will find the talk edifying; Apple have once again made a number of… interesting choices which will require significant engineering effort to integrate into upstream Mesa. It is well worth a watch if you’re interested in more detail. A huge thanks goes out to everyone who has made this work possible. More progress is on the way, so stay tuned. Kept you waiting, huh? All the way back in January of 2024, we made the mistake of promising Thunderbolt support within the year. It’s a mistake we won’t quickly repeat. We’ve said almost nothing about Thunderbolt in the two years since, which begs the question: where is it? It’s on the mailing list! Thunderbolt was originally developed by Apple and Intel, with Intel handling the design and fabrication of the hardware required. Since Intel made these controllers available to anyone who wanted them at a (mostly) reasonable price, no one else bothered to design their own. It is only very recently — largely coinciding with the transfer of the standard to the USB-IF — that companies like AMD have decided to roll their own controllers. Apple is of course no exception. As part of their push for insourcing most silicon IP, Apple made the choice to design their own Thunderbolt controller before most others. Surprising no one, the controller is of course a Cortex-M3 running RTKit coupled with a bespoke Thunderbolt/USB4 router. There is one of these for each Thunderbolt-enabled USB-C port on all Apple Silicon Macs. Since Intel supplies every other extant Thunderbolt controller on the market, the Linux kernel’s Thunderbolt subsystem is effectively designed around them. It makes a number of assumptions about the hardware topology of the running machine, including hardware capabilities and access patterns for certain registers and regions of shared memory. Apple’s controller breaks a lot of these assumptions. Great. The Thunderbolt controller is also oddly coupled to PMGR. The reset line for each controller is asserted or deasserted by setting and clearing a set of bits in the middle of PMGR’s MMIO range. No other hardware block works quite like this, and it took some time to realise that these seemingly random writes to PMGR were not just noise. Luckily for us, Sven was up to the task of dealing with all this nonsense. It just took slightly longer than expected! While the patchset to enable Thunderbolt was sent upstream first (another massive win for us!), we have also pulled it into our downstream kernel and are now shipping it to users! But there is a catch. Currently, only USB3, XDomain and Thunderbolt Networking are supported. You can plug in USB devices or connect two Thunderbolt computers together and make them ping each other, but that’s about it. PCIe and DisplayPort tunnelling — required for most Thunderbolt docks — are not supported. Yet. Watch this space. An enormous amount of gratitude is owed to Sven, who has stuck with this thankless chore for nearly 5 years in between all of his other incredible work. “The Holy Grail, Doctor Jones” Playing retail PC games on Asahi Linux is a bit of a pain point, to say the least. The software stack required to enable this is incredibly complex. We need to translate x86/amd64 binaries to arm64, and do so fast enough for low-latency gaming. In most cases, we also need to deal with the Windows API. On top of that, almost all games bake in an assumed 4 KiB memory page size to enable certain performance optimisation. Over the past few years, most of these problems have been solved: FEX has improved leaps and bounds. The performance and reliability of binary translation is hardly a consideration in most cases now; WINE is also fantastic now. Support for ARM64EC is mature and reliable, meaning that FEX now only has to translate the game binaries rather than WINE’s entire Windows API implementation; and muvm allows us to spin up a thin VM with DRM Native Context to present a 4 KiB memory page size to x86/amd64 applications. When muvm was first developed, it was with the assumption that DRM Native Context would enable near-native GPU performance from inside the VM. Unfortunately, this assumption did not hold. The muvm performance penalty is quite significant for a number of reasons, about 20% depending on the workload. Engineering around the limitations inherent to using a VM also introduces issues; muvm cannot use Wayland, has slow I/O performance, and struggles with certain types of input devices. This is one area where macOS has us completely licked. While the performance gap between FEX and Rosetta has narrowed, XNU allows userspace processes to map themselves at any page granularity, so all Rosetta needs to do is tell XNU to map 4 KiB pages for its child processes. Linux does not have this flexibility. All pages must be mapped at the same granularity as the kernel. While we did tease Windows games working outside of muvm last year, this relied on ugly hacks inside FEX which have since been removed in the interests of maintainability and translation correctness. Bummer. Even so, compatibility was hit-and-miss, with a lot of (mostly older) software still refusing to work. Double bummer. Android is currently going through a transition from 4 KiB pages to 16 KiB pages for a variety of reasons. Google Play now requires apps to be built for 16 KiB systems, and any application updates which do not test successfully on such systems will not be approved for publication on the Play Store. What about applications which are no longer updated though? What about sideloaded enterprise slop apps? Google engineers Kalesh Singh and Frederick Mayle gave a very interesting talk at Linux Plumbers Conference this year about exactly this. Their solution is simple: just fix Linux so that userspace can map 4 KiB pages! Their addition to the Android kernel is called P3S, or Per Process Page Size. On ARM64 systems, pagetable granularity is controlled by bits set in the Translation Control Registers (TCR). P3S works by tracking the granularity of each process’s pagetables, and writing the appropriate bits to the TCR whenever a process with a different pagetable size is switched to. Because this is a single register write, and because this is a no-op for “native” page size processes, the performance penalty is effectively zero! While this effort is primarily targeted at Android, the patchset mostly rebases cleanly on top of mainline Linux. What happens if we rebase it on top of our Asahi tree (and fix some bugs)? As it turns out: Star Wars Battlefront (2004) running outside of muvm, with WineD3D Okay okay, Battlefront is a very simple Direct3D 9.0 game from 22 years ago. Not exactly an impressive demo, right? Well what about: Wolfenstein: The New Order (2014) running outside of muvm Wolfenstein: The New Order is an extremely well-optimised OpenGL title, and being 64-bit uses WINE’s ARM64EC pathways to massively reduce the amount of work FEX has to do. Again, not exactly an impressive demo if we’re judging based on technical difficulty. Let’s find something else. Something… worse. Something 32-bit so that FEX and WINE have to work harder. Something that will exercise DXVK too. Something that is so comically buggy and poorly optimised that it doesn’t even work properly on real Windows machines, and relies on community patches and command line switches to start at all on modern computers: Grand Theft Auto IV (2008) running outside of muvm, with DXVK That’s more like it! But we can do even worse . We can even run… Bethesda games! Fallout: New Vegas (2010) running outside of muvm, with DXVK Performance is of course still patchy. Both Battlefront and Wolfenstein run essentially flawlessly, with the latter hitting 144+ FPS on an M2 Max Mac Studio. GTA IV on the other hand is… not fantastic. Performance is still massively improved over using muvm, and eliminating the use of the VM in general should also eliminate a few classes of bugs. Debugging the GPU driver should also be much easier with this approach. As always there is a catch, and unfortunately it’s a big one. The current solution is hard-coded for 16 KiB hosts and 4 KiB processes on those hosts. This obviously satisfies Google’s commercial requirements, but adding pagesize-specific kludges to the kernel’s core memory management code is not appropriate upstream. We are unsure if Google intends to generalise this approach and upstream it, or if this is going to stay an Android-only patchset. As such, we do not want to ship this in our downstream tree and have folks become reliant on it when there is this level of uncertainty. It also requires userspace integration. P3S works by checking the binary metadata for its sections’ page alignments. This works for Google’s use case, as P3S is intended as a fallback mechanism for applications aligned to 4 KiB pages. Modern arm64 binaries are aligned to 64 KiB however, as this guarantees compatibility with systems of all native pagesizes. Thus, a shim is required to force P3S on. The shim triggers P3S, and any child processes will inherit its 4 KiB pagesize. It is not worth spending the effort on implementing this until we have some certainty around what Google intends to do with this patchset. We have reached out to Google with some questions, and we hope to have more to say soon. Mics, but faster Our custom beamformer for the microphone array found in the MacBooks is written in Rust. Rust’s scientific computing ecosystem is not as mature as C++’s, which is a bit of a problem as beamforming requires realtime FFT and very heavy matrix operations to be done on buffers filled with audio samples. Mature scientific computing libraries have hand-optimised code, often using intrinsics tied to the target ISA. We were not doing this however, and relied on the compiler autovectorising code where it could to achieve our performance targets. This fell apart when we eliminated the FFT-based analytic transform, replacing it with an implementation based on infinite impulse response (IIR) filters. This should be faster, however the compiler was failing to autovectorise the new implementation. Linkmauve kindly stepped in and added SIMD-optimised code for both arm64 and amd64. This, coupled with other performance optimisations courtesy of Frédéric Bour has resulted in Triforce becoming almost twice as fast, all while using less CPU time! Keeping up Fedora Linux 45 was released on 3 November, and we shipped Fedora Asahi Remix on the same day. This is the first time we have been able to get a new version of Fedora Asahi Remix out on the same day as upstream! Learning from history We take great pride in our work, and have always done all of our development in the open. We communicate with our users, our followers and our financial sponsors as transparently as is humanly possible. Our finances are in the open, our development branches are in the open, and we report our progress regularly and candidly in the open. Our IRC channels and Matrix rooms are safe spaces, open to anyone with even a passing interest in Asahi Linux or hacking on Apple Silicon. We do all of this because we firmly believe in Free and Open Source Software, not just as a means to an end but as the end in and of itself. The modern digital world is only possible because of the Free Software movement, and it is more important now than it ever has been that we do all we can to protect the Free Software ecosystem and uphold the ideals upon which it is built. It may surprise some to learn that WINE was originally made available under the MIT licence. The 90s and 2000s were a very different time in the Free Software ecosystem, and permissively licenced projects were viewed by tech companies as free real estate to pilfer and exploit. WINE was not immune to this, and many monetised proprietary forks of WINE were marketed and sold by various bad actors. The WINE development team grew increasingly concerned that these proprietary forks, while well within their rights to exist, would eventually cause so much fragmentation in the ecosystem that WINE itself would become unviable. In 2002, WINE was relicenced under the LGPL to prevent further proprietary forks from being created, and to encourage direct upstream contribution. When Asahi Linux was first started, it was with the intent that we develop a Free Software ecosystem for the Apple Silicon platform. To facilitate and encourage the participation of our friends at the BSDs and other Free Software operating systems, we endeavoured to licence as much of our code as possible under the permissive MIT licence. Unfortunately, this is no longer viable. The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community. Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Until next time! As always, we would like to sincerely thank our supporters on OpenCollective and GitHub Sponsors . It is only through your generous backing that we are able to dedicate the time and resources to continuing our work reverse engineering the platform and bringing to it a world-class, polished, and battle-tested Linux desktop experience. You mean the world to us. James Calligeros · 2026-11-07 Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 Linux® is the registered trademark of Linus Torvalds in the U.S. and other countries. Boston Bay Area South Florida San Diego Connecticut tv Today Nightly News Meet the Press Dateline Featured NBC News Now Nightly Films Stay Tuned Special Features Newsletters Podcasts Listen Now Business in America More From NBC NBC.COM NBCU Academy Peacock NEXT STEPS FOR VETS NBC News Site Map Help Follow NBC News news Alerts There are no new alerts at this time Search Search Facebook Twitter Email SMS Blue Sky Whatsapp Print Reddit Flipboard Pinterest Linkedin Latest Stories Politics U.S. News World Sports Business Health Selected Tipline Tech News Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales in few markets Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Tesla to wind down production of Cybertruck 01:31 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 6, 2026, 8:36 AM EST / Source : Reuters By Reuters Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era." Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future." But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X. body_text: Kevin Boone: First steps in bare-metal programming using UEFI – series index Kevin Boone Home Contact About Software Articles 🔍 First steps in bare-metal programming using UEFI – series index These articles are about using a Linux workstation to develop bare-metal applications for a PC-type computer with UEFI firmware. They are written for experienced Linux developers, but assume no prior knowledge of UEFI. The articles cover the software tools needed, how to compile and link, how to create a bootable disk, and basic file management. Please note that I wrote these articles to be read in order. Each one relies on information from the previous articles, and it might be difficult to follow them out of sequence. Part 1 – Compiling and Linking Part 2 – The EFI system partition Part 3 – Making a DVD or USB flash image Part 4 – A pragmatic digression Part 5 – Handling files using the Simple File Protocol Have you posted something in response to this page? title: Running a law firm on Free software
body_text: Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition) | decoded.legal's blog " /> decoded.legal's blog Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition) Published on: 2026-11-06 12:18:47 by Neil Brown I started running decoded.legal - a small English law firm, focussing on Internet, telecoms, and tech law - on Free software, both client and server side, around five years ago. I have used Free software in my personal life for a lot longer than that. Back in 2022, I wrote about my experiences after the first year or so . I wrote an update in 2024 . Someone asked me recently what I am doing now, and, while it is mostly the same, some bits have changed. So here is the 2026 update. Client-side stuff I am still using Debian, with GNOME, and it works well for me. Iâm using it on a ThinkPad X1 Yoga Gen 6 , as my primary machine, and, being a âYogaâ version, I rather like being able to fold the screen back and write on it to mark up documents. ( Here are my thoughts on the different âActive Pensâ available for it .) However, the machine itself seems to have a hardware problem with the Thunderbolt / USB-C ports (fine for power, very flaky for data), and so I might need to replace it. And I have no idea what laptop I might get. Email (MUA): Thunderbird and mutt , depending on what I am doing Quick Folder Move and Move Message And Yourself are particularly useful add-ons for Thunderbird, for rapid filing of email with keyboard shortcuts Thunderbird seems to be having a problem with some recurring calendar invitations, while ikhal is handling them fine. Iâve not dug into it, but it is a nuisance. Document production: LibreOfficeâs Writer if I want a âWordâ document (e.g.Â I am exchanging documents with other lawyers), and I am using pandoc and typst to convert Markdown files that I tend to write in vim for some other bits. Iâd like to explore tex at some point, as I have a client who likes diffs to their .tex files, and that looks rather neat. Presentations: reveal.js I absolutely love this. I have a bash script which sets up a template for a new presentation, and then I just write the presentation using Markdown. I get a nicely-formatted presentation (using a css template) with very little effort, and no distracting GUI Blogpost about reveal.js Here are some presentations Iâve given, using reveal.js File manager: Nautilus Mainly because it is GNOMEâs default, although, especially when combined with some useful bash scripts , it works well for my needs PDFs: evince for most reading; Xournal++ for marking up PDFs; PDFarranger and pdftk for interfering with PDFs Text expansion: espanso This is a fantastic shortcut for me, saving me from typing the same thing multiple times. I have loads of shortcuts set up, and Iâd be lost without them. Browser: Firefox or links I am still using Firefox. It is â¦ fine? I should probably look at LibreWolf or another fork, as Iâm not enamoured by Mozillaâs direction of travel but, for now, Firefox it is. I use Firefox for joining peopleâs Teams and Zoom etc. meetings, if someone else sets up the meeting, and that works fine Local wiki / knowledge management: vimwiki because I use vim so much, vimwiki was quite an obvious choice. I use this for keeping track of my professional development, and for various notes Disk encryption: LUKS Client-side encryption of files before syncing them with Syncthing : Cryptomator Fediverse: I tend to use the Mastodon advanced web UI or, when I want fewer images, the TUI toot . I schedule toots - for example, about blogposts, using a simple bash script and a cron job ; it has moved on a bit since I wrote that post, but it is the same principle Password manager: Bitwarden , using the vaultwarden server, with YubiKeys for managing more sensitive credentials Markdown editor (for blogposts; I do presentations in vim or gedit): Apostrophe Scanning: paperless-ngx Label printing: thereâs a great FOSS web UI for Brother (and perhaps other) label printers . I donât print many labels, as we aim to be paperless, but itâs convenient when I need to do so Why so many terminal-based tools? The simple answer is that I am very comfortable in a terminal, and I like them. They have fewer distractions and, when compared with most GUI software, are just - IMHO - easier to use, especially when I donât need to move my hands away from the keyboard. So, while I donât use them exclusively, I use mutt , vim , ikhal , ncmpcpp , newsboat , toot , links , and various other TUIs, frequently. Server-side stuff Everything here - other than Signal - is self-hosted, and Iâm mostly using Intel NUCs now. I still have some Raspberry Pi devices, but fewer than I did. (Again, this doesnât list everything; just the main applications.) Email (MTA): postfix / dovecot I need to move our mail infrastructure at some point, and I want to look at Stalwart. File synchronisation: Syncthing One of the bigger changes since last time was moving away from Nextcloud. I just was not getting on with it, and it was causing me more problems than it solved. So I switched to Syncthing for file sync, and radicale for CalDAV / CardDAV. Iâve been more than happy with this combination. Video conferencing: Signal I ran jitsi for years, but stopped using it a few months back. Jitsi is great, and I remain a fan, but most of the time I am joining other peopleâs Teams or Zoom meetings, so I was running the Jitsi server for very little usage. I turned it off, and instead offer Signal. I have had no grumbles. Invoicing and tracking payments: InvoicePlane , just for generating PDF invoices. Clients donât interact with it Time tracking: Kimai v2 of Kimai is excellent, and I had a very pleasant exchange with the developer, which is always nice. âCase managementâ / âMatter managementâ: EspoCRM VPN: WireGuard , using trailofbitâs algo ansible scripts on one machine, and PiVPN on another (albeit not on a Pi) Vulnerability scanning: greenbone/OpenVAS Monitoring: Uptime Kuma I implemented this not long after the last update. It â¦ just works? Forge / hosted git repository: Forgejo I use this for version tracking the website, and for a couple of template projects I do not host anything particularly important on it - for that, I have a git process running on another machine, which is not accessible over the Internet, and I just push to that SIEM: Wazuh Password manager: vaultwarden Website: it is a static site built via mkdocs , hosted on apache2 It got even simpler and even faster to load. Yes, itâs basic, but I like it! We still have an .onion version . If you visit decoded.legal in Tor Browser, it should re-direct your automatically Blog: BSSG After a couple of annoyances with hugo, I moved to BSSG - a bash static site generator. The developer, Stefano, is amazing, and it is working incredibly well. Iâve gone for a very basic, easy to read, theme - which should be very similar to what was there before - and thereâs still an RSS feed for it, of course I blog quite frequently, and, rather than keep private / internal âknowhowâ files, I tend to just blog things and share the learnings I tend to use my personal blog for posts about the more technical bits and pieces I have automated the most common actions - templates, and publishing - using bash scripts, so that I can focus on writing (in Markdown); getting it online is the easiest bit Fediverse: I am using the *glitch-soc Mastodon** fork Switching from normal Mastodon to glitch-soc Mastodon was easy I stopped using Markdown in toots, even though I like the rendered output (i.e.Â as html not as markdown), but this is not supported consistently well across clients, so I stopped using it. I turned off decoded.legalâs own fedi instance. I had been on the fence as to whether this is worthwhile or not for a while, and decided that, really, it was not. Knowledge management, and managing our law firmâs (numerous) policies and procedures: dokuwiki with the Markdown plugin DNS: unbound , with Pi-Hole in front of it I used to run a doh server, but Iâve stopped doing that. Backups: restic and rsync Notes on restic Forms: LiberaForms I have been really happy with LiberaForms, for easy-to-create and easy-to-use forms, especially since they implemented encryption, so that the form responses are stored encrypted on the server. I still delete them as soon as I can, but knowing that they are encrypted in the database is welcome. I use LiberaForms for our âKnow Your Clientâ pre-engagement questionnaire, and for various other bits Collaborative document editing: I donât. I used to run CryptPad, but it just didnât get much use, so I turned it off. AI tools None, for various reasons . Mobile device Iâm using a Pixel running GrapheneOS for my mobile device. I use F-Droid as the main app store. Using Android doesnât thrill me, especially given Googleâs direction of travel, but at the moment - despite trying quite a lot of different OSs and devices, including postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch, as well as SailfishOS previously - I have not found something that does what I need better than GrapheneOS. Working with others (who donât use FOSS tools) No change here: zero problems. Many of my clients use Microsoftâs software, or Appleâs software. Linux tech Debian law firm FOSS Free software Related Posts Running a law firm on Free software (2024 edition) Would you like a decoded.legal holiday card? (2025 edition) Running a law firm on Linux - a year or so in All posts CC BY-SA-NC 4.0 or any later version, unless otherwise stated. This blog is for interest only; nothing here is legal advice. title: Kugelblitz – Mac-Native Google Earth Alternative
body_text: Kugelblitz · Metaebene Applications Skip to content Metaebene Applications Applications Blog About DE EN Kugelblitz A library. A spaceship. A time machine. App for macOS Download 1.1 DMG · 76.2 MB · macOS 27 or later · Apple silicon Overview Features Release notes The Earth and its neighbors as a 3D globe and atlas for the Mac – maps and open geodata on real terrain. Kugelblitz shows the Earth and its neighbors as a globe and as an atlas you fly over smoothly like a pilot, even on an M1. Imagery, road map and topographic map lie on real terrain, joined by thousands of open maps from the Library. Everything comes from freely available geodata, straight from its publishers, OpenStreetMap from the Kugelblitz tile server; you need no account. Everything loaded stays in the cache, and Kugelblitz instances in the same network share it with each other if you wish. Status windows tell how far the view has loaded, where you are looking and where its data comes from, and every source is listed with its license in “Sources and Licenses”. Kugelblitz speaks German and English and uses the units of your choice. Drawn maps on real terrain The Earth on three kinds of map, as a globe and as an atlas: Imagery, road map and topographic map. The two drawn ones do not lie flat beside it but on the globe's terrain, with buildings in 3D. A scene brings back a ready-made view in one move. More about Maps → Every body flat as a printed map Beside the globe Kugelblitz shows every body as an atlas: the same data flat in five projections, from the whole sheet to the finest images. You switch in the title bar or with ⇧⌘A. More about Atlas → Search, view and add the world's open geodata The Library (⇧⌘B) opens directories and geoportals with map services from all over the world: aerial images, satellite images, elevation models, maps and buildings in 3D. “On the Globe” shows any service at once, and one click adds it to “My Places”. More about Library → All of OpenStreetMap, without a download and without regions OpenStreetMap comes from Kugelblitz's own tile server: the whole planet, prepared for Kugelblitz, in tiles only for the area you see, at the level the distance asks for. No regions, no large download, the same everywhere on Earth. More about Tile server → Fly like a pilot with a SpaceMouse The SpaceMouse from 3Dconnexion is Kugelblitz's control stick: all movements at once, as fine as you move the cap, without a driver. Keyboard, trackpad and mouse work as well, all at once too. More about Flying → Smooth, even on an M1 Aerial image, terrain, buildings, roads and names at once, and the flight stays smooth. Kugelblitz is made and measured on a Mac mini with M1 and 16 GB. More about Performance → The Mac streams the globe into the headset The Mac draws, the headset shows: View → “Show on Vision Pro…” (⌥⌘V) brings the globe all around you, without an app on the headset, from an M1 too. Checked with Mac and headset on 27.2. More about Apple Vision Pro → What happened, where and when Eclipses over 5,000 years, computed rather than read from tables, as well as earthquakes, eruptions, tsunamis and fireballs at their place and time. Let the time shuttle run and you see them come and go. title: They don't make 'em like that any more: Borland Turbo Pascal 7
body_text: Kevin Boone: They don’t make ’em like that any more: Borland Turbo Pascal 7 Kevin Boone Home Contact About Software Articles 🔍 They don’t make ’em like that any more: Borland Turbo Pascal 7 Borland’s Turbo Pascal was one of the most successful programming tools of all time. It introduced development techniques, such as integrated source-level debugging, that we take for granted today; but which were radical at the time. TP 7, also known as Turbo Pascal for Windows 1.5 , was the pinnacle of the Turbo Pascal line, and its end. The name ‘Turbo’ was associated with what were regarded as hobbyist products – ‘Borland Pascal’ was a different, much more expensive, product. But Turbo Pascal was enough for some quite substantial applications, and was very affordable. It was also ‘book licensed’, which I think was a new thing in the software industry. You could buy one copy of TP, and any number of people could use it – but only one at a time. Even when it was distributed on floppy disks, there was no copy protection. (Turbo) Pascal eventually gave way to Delphi which, despite its technical merits, never had the same impact. I used TP 7 to write medical imaging software back in the 90s, to run under Windows 3.1 – which was a great operating system in its day. Like previous releases, Windows 3.1 was still, essentially, an extension to MSDOS, but with clever tricks to allow it to multitask (after a fashion) and address more memory. It had a simple, consistent user interface model – both for the user and the programmer. It had, at that time, none of the wasteful and irritating anti-features that have come to make modern Windows so depressing to use. So Windows 3.1 was a platform we all wanted our applications to support – not that there were many alternatives at that time. Like many other programmers, I learned the Pascal programming language specifically to use TP 7 – I was essentially a C programmer in those days, but programming for Windows in C was a horrible job. Frankly, it’s scarcely better today. It was, and is, necessary to combine a whole stack of command-line tools that take incomprehensible text files as input. TP 7 automated and concealed all that nastiness. It wasn’t just the tools that were a problem: the user interface model was, essentially, object-oriented; but C did not make it easy to program in an object-oriented way. TP 5 had introduced basic object-oriented concepts to the Pascal language, and these were were to prove essential. The Windows-specific features were provided by something called Object Windows Library : a relatively thick, object-oriented wrapper around the basic Windows C API. My recollection is that Borland introduced an object-oriented programming library for Microsoft Windows before Microsoft did – and Borland’s was better. Turbo Pascal running in Windows 3.1 OWL made it easy to create nice-looking user interfaces, with a bit of eye candy. The familiar ‘green tick button’ was an OWL enhancement, which graced so many Windows applications that it eventually became an irritating cliche. All, in all, It was much easier to program for Windows using Turbo Pascal 7 than with anything else. Not only did it provide a programming model that matched the way the Windows user interface worked, the application itself had a Windows graphical interface – many Windows programming tools at that time actually ran under MSDOS, and were entirely text-based. TP 7 also had fully-graphical tools for designing the user interface elements, like menus and icons. Laying out a menu using a definition file with an obscure format, using Windows Notepad, was never an agreeable experience. Microsoft did produce graphical tools for this kind of operation, but Turbo Pascal combined them into a seamless IDE. All I had to do to build and run my programs was to hit the F7 key. I could even set breakpoints for the debugger, just by clicking a line of code. As I said, common enough today, but revolutionary for early Windows programming. But what really made TP 7 special was its CP/M heritage. Turbo Pascal came to Windows by way of CP/M and MSDOS, which meant it had a compiler core that was designed to run with tight memory and a comparatively slow CPU. In the days when most compilers had to write a stack of intermediate files on disk, TP just constructed everything in memory. It did this using highly-optimized code, written in assembly language, by very skilled people. It doesn’t matter much today if your compiler spits out a heap of temporary files, because disk storage is fast and cheap. But in the days of the floppy disk, you had to minimize disk access. Unfortunately, you also had to minimize memory use, because there wasn’t much of that, either. Programming for CP/M took real skill and dedication. So when TP came to Windows machines, with their 16-bit CPUs and megabytes of RAM, it was like an early Christmas for developers. A compiler designed to be adequate with 32kB of RAM and a single floppy drive will positively fly when given megabytes and a hard disk. All this meant that TP 7 was a joy to use. It was like a modern IDE, but without any of the bloat. Developers who would never have tackled Windows programming with Microsoft tools were able to move from MSDOS to Windows without too much difficulty – even if they first had to learn Pascal, as I did. The compiled code was pretty speedy but, if it wasn’t brisk enough, you could write assembly language directly in the Pascal source files. I don’t think it’s too much of an exaggeration to claim that Turbo Pascal contributed to the widespread uptake, and eventual domination, of Microsoft Windows on desktop PCs. If there had been a ‘Turbo Pascal for Linux’ in the early 90s, then we might all be running Linux on our desktops today. So what happened to Turbo Pascal? Three things, at least, contributed to its eventual downfall. First, there was increasing competition from the C programming language. Borland did produce a Turbo C, and later a Turbo C++, but they weren’t as influential as Pascal. It’s easy to forget that PCs weren’t the first general-purpose computing devices. Most scientific and educational establishments, and many businesses, used graphical workstations and a central minicomputer. C was already well-established in these environments before desktop computers started to become prominent. And before that we had mainframes and terminals – but that was a different world, where Fortran and COBOL ruled. Most ‘serious’ PC applications were written in assembly language in the early days, as they had been for CP/M – the low resources almost necessitated this. Minicomputers were not so limited, so compilers were more practicable, even in the 1980s. So when compilers started to become of interest to microcomputer developers, there was almost no reason to favour one programming language over another. Pascal could have become the standard programming language for the PC. That it did not, I think, reflects the fact that many software companies that had been active in industrial and scientific computing saw an opportunity in PCs, and tried to move into that market. These companies already had substantial experience with C, and they brought their preferences with them. So while I was happy to learn a new programming language to develop for Windows, a software business with a thousand staff might not have wanted to take that step. The second factor, I think, was the increasing palatability of Microsoft’s C tools. Microsoft did eventually produce an IDE of its own and, of course, Microsoft controlled the Windows platform. I don’t think Microsoft’s C IDEs ever became as easy to use as Borland’s, but they probably didn’t have to, given Microsoft’s position. Third, Microsoft’s Visual BASIC started to attact small-scale and bespoke developers. BASIC was already a staple of the microcomputing world, because it was easy to learn, and did not require a separate compilation step. Attaching bits of BASIC code to Windows user interface elements was an efficient way to produce relatively simple, small-volume applications. I loathed Visual BASIC in the 90s, and I loathed it until the day VB6 drew its last laboured, wheezing breath in 2005. Still, I can’t deny its popularity, and I’m sure that many of the same people who were drawn to Turbo Pascal were later drawn to Visual BASIC, for much the same reasons. VB lowered the barriers to entry into Windows programming in the same way that TP had previously done. Arguably it lowered them too much, but let’s not go there today. Early versions of Turbo Pascal are now freely, and legally, available. Retrocomputing enthusiasts with an interest in early PCs and MSDOS are well catered for. So far as I know, however, TP 7 remains somebody’s intellectual property, although it isn’t entirely clear whose. It probably comes into the category of ‘abandonware’ but, to be frank, it’s not all that important: it can’t produce code that runs on modern Windows systems, and few people have much interest in early Windows – it’s just not retro enough. So that’s Turbo Pascal: a colossus of the microcomputing world, which faded and died largely unlamented. It always was a creature of its time – it prospered for the brief period when microcomputers were limited enough to reward skilled development, but widespread enough to create a substantial market for programmers. By the time it started to become difficult to find enough highly-skilled programmers to satisfy the market needs, it didn’t matter: computers were getting powerful enough to make good our limitations as programmers. That almost nobody has the skills these days to implement something like TP is something we could eventually come to regret – or, rather, our grandchildren could. Software development is becoming a semi-skilled industry, and I doubt that the rise of AI will entirely compensate for this. But who needs a Turbo Pascal, when you have 128Gb of RAM attached to an 5GHz CPU, for a hastily-written, bloated Java program to burn? Have you posted something in response to this page? People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. Contents Part I: Welcome What BUI is Why BUI exists Who it's for Pick your language Features at a glance A gallery Part II: Getting started Install First app: tkinter First app: Blender components First app: Qt syntax First app: Rust, in rsx and gpui builders First app: JavaScript and React First app: Dear ImGui First app: C Part III: Concepts How it works Blender's widgets and interactions Three looks: HTML, styled and Blender components Rendering on the CPU and the GPU Damage rendering Window hosts Text and fonts Themes: dark and light Part IV: Guides by language Python Rust JavaScript and React Dear ImGui C and embedding Lua Where the docs live Part V: Performance Before you read the numbers Start time and battery Frame times JavaScript and React: startup and animation Run the benchmarks yourself Part VI: Reference Platforms Environment variables Building from source and CMake options Coverage Repository layout Examples Part VII: The project Status and roadmap FAQ Contributing and publishing License and credits Part I: Welcome 1. What BUI is BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit : a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings : thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language , but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc , and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. 2. Why BUI exists Blender's interface is famous for how it feels . You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. 3. Who it's for You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations : no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system. 4. On crates.io : cargo add blenderui . Fast by design Damage rendering : an idle UI costs 0% CPU, and a hover redraws only the widget it touches. Opt-in GPU renderer (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux), modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing. It draws the same pixels as the CPU raster. In the benchmark, 2–4× less CPU per frame than gpui-fast , with less RAM and a ~5 ms first frame . Blender's text : Inter (Blender's UI font) is embedded and rendered with FreeType the way Blender renders it, so text looks the same on every platform. On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug , falling back to a per-glyph atlas like Blender's. Images One decoder set for every language , in C: PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA, QOI ( Wuffs , memory-safe), JPEG (libjpeg-turbo), WebP including animated (libwebp), Radiance HDR, PNM and SVG. The design is Blender's imbuf: one image type and a format table. Decoded at the size it is drawn, off the UI thread : JPEG thumbnails use DCT scaling (a 4K photo becomes a 256 px thumbnail in ~12 ms), visible images first, scrolled-away requests cancelled, and only the image's rectangle redraws when it arrives. The page never jumps: sizes come from the file header. One memory-budgeted cache (256 MiB by default). Scrolling 1,000 photo thumbnails: 2.9 ms p99 frames and 100 MB , against 96 ms and 2.5 GB when decoding on the UI thread; 0 allocations in a settled frame, every block freed at exit. Images . Animated GIF and WebP play everywhere an image shows, decoded one frame at a time at the size drawn (two frames held per animation), each frame for its own delay, only the image's rectangle repainting. Off screen, scrolled away or in a hidden window they pause: 200 animations at once take 0.76 ms p50 / 1.5 ms p99 render frames, and nothing at all once off screen. frame holds one frame; reduced motion holds them all. Large images on the GPU : images over 2047 px get a texture of their own on Direct3D 11 and OpenGL (tiled only past the device limit), freed with the image. Video : <video> in every language, decoded by the OS (Media Foundation with DXVA, GStreamer, AVFoundation; loaded at run time) at the size drawn, frames in one GPU texture per player updated in place, YCbCr converted in the shader, and nothing decoded off screen . 1080p plays at 0.99 ms render frames and 9 % of a core on the GPU renderer, five at once at 28 %, with 0 allocations per frame . Play, pause, seek, rate, loop, poster, state events, and Blender-style controls. Install Python. You need CPython 3.11 or newer. Wheels are published for Windows, Linux and macOS, so there's nothing to compile. One package gives you all four Python APIs (tkinter syntax, Qt syntax, the Blender components and Dear ImGui): pip install blenderui python -c " import blenderui; print(blenderui.__version__) " Import it as blenderui . You'll also see import bui in older examples: it's the same code under its original name, but an unrelated project owns bui on PyPI, so prefer blenderui in anything you publish. Rust. The crate is blenderui on crates.io : cargo add blenderui The first build compiles BUI's C kit for you, so you need Rust 1.88 or newer, CMake and a C compiler (on Windows, the Visual Studio Build Tools for the default MSVC target), and on Linux the X11 headers ( libx11-dev or libX11-devel ; no GL headers are needed). JavaScript. You need Node.js 18 or newer, or Bun: npm install @blender-ui/react react # or: bun add @blender-ui/react react npm install @blender-ui/svelte svelte # Svelte 5 npm install @blender-ui/native # the DOM-like API, without React The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 , Linux x64 (glibc 2.35 or later; native X11 windows) and macOS . Elsewhere, build the addon from a clone ( npm install then npm run build in bindings/ , with Rust, CMake and a C compiler). On macOS , JavaScript runs headless for now (see Platforms ). C and C++. Build from source with CMake 3.20+ and a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC or MinGW-w64, or Clang); on Linux, also the X11 headers: git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j 2 ctest --test-dir build # optional: run the test suites In your own CMake project, add BUI as a subdirectory and link bui::kit (or bui::imgui for Dear ImGui): add_subdirectory ( BUI ) target_link_libraries ( myapp PRIVATE bui::kit ) Dear ImGui. Python gets it with pip install blenderui ( import blenderui.imgui ). C++ links bui::imgui , C links bui_cimgui . Rust uses the blenderui-imgui crate: cargo add blenderui-imgui If something goes wrong: Symptom Fix ImportError: buipy You're running from a source checkout without a build. Build first ( cmake --build build ), or set BUIPY_BUILD_DIR . The extension must match your Python version. The window never appears Start the event loop: mainloop() , app.exec() or App.run() . Blurry or tiny UI Set BUI_UI_SCALE , for example BUI_UI_SCALE=1.25 . gpu=True does nothing Run with BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 to see why the GPU device didn't start. Without Direct3D 11 or OpenGL 3.3, BUI stays on the CPU renderer, which draws the same pixels. More: docs/getting-started.md and Install BUI on the website. 8. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c : a slider and a button in a native window. #include <stdio.h> #include "BUI_kit.h" static void on_event ( void * data , BKNode * node , int kind , void * ref , double a , double b ) { if ( kind == BK_EV_CLICK ) printf ( "clicked %s\n" , BK_get_str ( node , "text" )); else if ( kind == BK_EV_CHANGE ) printf ( "%s = %g\n" , BK_get_str ( node , "label" ), BK_get_num ( node , "value" )); } int main ( void ) { BKNode * root = BK_node_new ( "frame" ); /* everything is a node */ BK_set_num ( root , "padding" , 8 ); /* configured by property name */ BKNode * size = BK_node_new ( "slider" ); BK_set_str ( size , "label" , "Size" ); BK_set_num ( size , "max" , 10 ); BK_set_num ( size , "value" , 2.5 ); BK_node_add ( root , size , -1 ); BK_geom_set_manager ( size , BK_GEOM_PACK ); /* Tk's packer, in C */ BK_geom_set ( size , "fill" , 1 ); BKNode * apply = BK_node_new ( "button" ); BK_set_str ( apply , "text" , "Apply" ); BK_node_add ( root , apply , -1 ); BK_geom_set_manager ( apply , BK_GEOM_PACK ); BKContext * ctx = BK_context_new ( root ); /* input, focus, popups, undo */ BKHost host = { 0 }; host . emit = on_event ; /* the window fills in the rest */ BK_context_set_host ( ctx , & host ); if ( BK_window_supported ()) { /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */ BKWindow * win = BK_window_new ( ctx , "BUI from C" , 320 , 120 ); BK_window_show ( win ); BK_window_run (); BK_window_free ( win ); } BK_context_free ( ctx ); BK_node_free ( root ); return 0 ; } cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello The window below is a bigger program than the one above, a modifier stack: A bigger C program: a modifier stack ( examples/site/kit_modifiers.c ) Without a window system, render into a raster instead ( BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full) ), which is also how tests and screenshots work. Guide: docs/c-api.md . Part III: Concepts 15. How it works your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) Your code , in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc ( round_box_edges , widgetbase_draw , the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc . Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib , copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works . 16. Rendering on the CPU and the GPU BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels . The software raster ( gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c ) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows ( BUI_RASTER_THREADS ). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory. The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows ( gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c ) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux ( gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c ). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL , libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing. On both platforms the device starts on a worker thread, and the first frames draw on the CPU. The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends. Turn the GPU on: Where How Python bui.set_gpu(True) before creating windows; tkinter syntax also tk.Tk(gpu=True) Rust Application::new().gpu(true) , or WindowOptions { gpu: Some(true), .. } JavaScript new App({ gpu: true }) , or React's render(..., { gpu: true }) C BUI_gpu_set_default(1) , or BK_window_set_gpu(win, 1) Any app, no code change BUI_GPU=1 BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU ( BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why). Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon). More: Rendering . 19. Damage rendering Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window. A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow). Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window). If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer. Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles. The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing. Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage , Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles). On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering . 20. Window hosts A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input. Host Where Notes Win32 ( kit_window_win32.c ) Windows BUI's own host. Per-monitor DPI, vsync-paced animation, clipboard, cursors, window-manager features. X11 ( kit_window_x11.c ) Linux (also Wayland, via XWayland) Input mapping after Blender's GHOST. Xft.dpi scaling. libX11 is loaded when the first window opens. Wayland ( kit_window_wayland.c ) Linux, experimental Native Wayland windows, after Blender's GHOST_SystemWayland : xdg-shell, server-side decorations when offered, wl_seat with xkbcommon, clipboard, cursors, buffer scale, frame callbacks. CPU renderer only: with the GPU renderer on ( BUI_GPU=1 ) a Wayland session keeps using X11 through XWayland. BUI_WINDOW_BACKEND=x11|wayland picks one. libwayland loads at run time (Blender's wayland_dynload ). Needs the Wayland headers to build; without them Linux windows are X11 only. It's checked by CI and has been tried by hand on three Macs (two Apple Silicon, one Intel); testing notes in docs/macos-testing.md . Text and fonts Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's: Inter , Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1. Rendered like Blender's BLF : BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF , stb_truetype rasterizes instead. On the GPU , glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's ( BUI_SLUG=0 , bui.set_slug(False) , .slug(false) , BUI_gpu_set_slug(0) ). Other fonts : BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files. Windows' GDI text is opt-in ( -DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON , Rust feature gdi-text ): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug. Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), IME on Windows only (X11 and macOS are coming), right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. React and Svelte, side by side (one session, runs interleaved, medians of 3; --svelte in the commands below): 3,000 cells, one session (Node 26 / Bun 1.4 / QuickJS) CPU per frame RAM JavaScript per update Plain JS 37.0 / 37.4 / 38.6 ms 92 / 81 / 59 MB 14 / 13 / 28 µs React with signals 37.6 / 38.4 / 37.8 ms 100 / 87 / 60 MB 23 / 17 / 40 µs Svelte with signals (as values) 39.0 / 36.8 / 38.5 ms 116 / 97 / 75 MB 17 / 19 / 36 µs Svelte with runes 39.4 / 35.9 / 37.0 ms 117 / 98 / 75 MB 65 / 76 / 790 µs React with state 38.1 ms on Node 166 MB on Node 5.2 / 8.6 / 76 ms First frame, median of 12 React Svelte Svelte before RAM (React / Svelte) QuickJS executable ( bui build ) 93 ms 89 ms 81 ms 20.4 / 20.4 MB Bun executable ( --bun ) 106 ms 90 ms 94 ms 37.8 / 38.8 MB Bun ( --preload …/register ) 107 ms 121 ms 203 ms 36.5 / 40.2 MB Node.js ( --import …/register ) 125 ms 135 ms 393 ms 52.1 / 55.4 MB Every variant ran at 26–29 FPS in this session (the machine, not the code), so CPU per frame is mostly BUI's own rendering and differs within noise. "JavaScript per update" is the cost of one update alone: 500 back to back, each applied by the framework and sent to the UI thread. Svelte with signals costs what React with signals does: a BUI signal passed as a value ( {label} , style={style} ) binds its node, so an update skips Svelte. Before this release's work it went through Svelte as a store: 86–87 µs on Node.js and Bun, 793 µs on QuickJS. Svelte with runes pays Svelte's flush, which walks the component's effects (3,000 here): 65–76 µs, 790 µs on QuickJS (85 / 78 / 790 before). Memory: Svelte keeps 10–17 MB more than React with signals (6 MB less than before on Node). A heap snapshot puts the rest in Svelte's own effects, closures and each-block items, about 1.9 KB per cell; BUI's nodes are the same for both. Startup: register serves Svelte's runtime bundled (once, with Bun, into node_modules/.cache ), which brought Node.js from 393 to 135 ms and Bun from 203 to 121 ms. React and Svelte ran one after the other here. React with state on Bun and QuickJS: the 500 back-to-back re-renders overran the warm-up, so only its per-update cost is valid from this session. Bun also sometimes crashes when a React app quits (after its first frame), a bug that predates this work. Method, the memory breakdown and how to rerun: docs/javascript.md . 34. Where a variable and an app-wide API call set the same thing, the variable wins. Variable What it does BUI_GPU 1 draws native windows on the GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3). Overrides bui.set_gpu() , Application::gpu() , BUI_gpu_set_default() . 0 turns those defaults off; a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. BUI_SLUG GPU text: 1 from glyph outlines (Slug, the default), 0 from a per-glyph atlas. BUI_GPU_DEBUG 1 prints why the GPU renderer couldn't start. BUI_GPU_WARP 1 (Windows) creates the Direct3D 11 device on WARP, the software rasterizer. Handy in VMs and CI. BUI_GPU_MAX_TEXTURE Testing: the largest texture side the GPU renderers give one image (at least 64), so images over it are tiled as on devices with a small limit. BUI_GPU_EGL default or surfaceless (Linux): the EGL platform for offscreen GPU rendering. BUI_RASTER_THREADS 1 to 8 (Windows): the most threads the software raster uses for big canvases. Status and roadmap Known limitations. Read these before you pick BUI for something you will ship. The tables below have the details. No accessibility support. BUI draws its own widgets and does not talk to the platform's accessibility APIs (UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS), so screen readers can't see them. Don't use it for software that has to be accessible. Accessibility is planned. Text. Blender's bundled Inter font only (system fonts only with the Windows GDI option). No per-glyph font fallback (missing characters show as boxes), input methods (IME) on Windows only, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, and no OpenType features. It doesn't look native. BUI looks like Blender: its Dark and Light themes (other Blender theme files can't be loaded yet). It doesn't follow your operating system's theme, accent color or fonts. Rendering. The CPU rasterizer is the default and works everywhere. The optional GPU renderer is Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL 3.3 on Linux. There is none on macOS (no Metal): macOS always draws on the CPU. Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends don't exist yet. Platforms. Windows and Linux (X11; Wayland is experimental) are the supported ones. macOS works too: checked by CI and tried by hand on three Macs (two Apple Silicon, one Intel), though JavaScript windows are headless there. The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64, Linux x64 (glibc 2.35+) and macOS. Retained mode, no visual editor. BUI keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI; it is not an immediate-mode library. There is no drag-and-drop UI designer: you write the UI in code. Performance numbers come from one machine, a Windows 11 laptop (Ryzen 7 5800U). Linux and macOS haven't been measured yet. The home page demos are browser sketches, not the native engine (the page says so). Run the Python, Rust or JavaScript examples to feel the real widgets. A WebAssembly build is planned. It's a port, not Blender unchanged. Widget drawing and interaction are ported from Blender's UI sources, with edits (each marked BUI: ), and the rest of Blender (its data system, window manager and operators) isn't included. There is no automated sync with Blender's releases. Partial areas: Qt syntax (about 24%), CSS (261 of 745 properties render), video has no audio, and image formats such as AVIF, EXR, TIFF, JPEG XL and HEIC aren't supported. License. GPL: a program that includes BUI is distributed under the GPL too ( why ).
