Like a good render, it's done when the noise goes away. 42. FAQ Do I need Blender installed? No. BUI contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. Is it really my unchanged tkinter app? Yes. blenderui-tk app.py makes import tkinter return BUI's implementation, which covers every public tkinter and ttk name. Nine real programs are tested to behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. See the limitations for the few differences. Is it a web browser in Rust? No. There's no browser engine and no network. BUI takes HTML elements and CSS as a UI language : they are laid out with taffy and drawn by BUI's engine, with Blender's widgets where you ask for them, in a native window. JavaScript is optional: the Rust crate needs none, and the JavaScript packages drive the same engine. Is the Dear ImGui support a re-implementation? No. It's the real Dear ImGui (vendored, MIT), running on a BUI backend, so every function behaves as upstream. The optional Blender-widgets build swaps only how ImGui's widgets are drawn and how they react to the mouse, by compiling an edited copy of imgui_widgets.cpp . How is it different from Electron, Electrobun or GPUIX? Electron ships Chromium with every app: on the order of 100 MB or more. Electrobun runs on Bun and renders in the system's webview. It's small to download, but the UI is still a browser page. GPUIX , like BUI, renders React natively: React drives Zed's GPUI. BUI also renders natively, with Blender's widgets, a much larger part of CSS, Tailwind, and hooks backed by signals. bui build makes a 5 MB executable that reaches its first frame in about 70 ms. Do the macros cost performance? rsx! , #[component] , css! and tw! expand at compile time into the same builder calls you would write by hand. Tailwind classes are compiled to CSS once, on first use. Hooks are a few nanoseconds per read or write. Can I change the colors? Yes. Switch between Blender's Dark and Light themes at run time ( Themes ), color individual widgets in every API, and use full CSS on plain HTML elements in Rust and JavaScript. Loading any other Blender theme file is coming soon. Does it run on my Mac? Yes. The Cocoa host works: it has been tried by hand on three Macs, two Apple Silicon and one Intel (the bugs they found are fixed), and CI builds and tests it on Apple Silicon and Intel runners. It draws on the CPU (there is no Metal renderer), and JavaScript windows are headless there. Python can always fall back to the Tk window ( BUI_HOST=tk ). If you try it, the notes in docs/macos-testing.md say what to report. Can I use BUI from Vue, Angular, Ruby, Go or Lua? Lua is now supported: cmake -DBUI_BUILD_LUA_BINDINGS=ON builds bui-lua (a standalone host) and bui.so / bui.dll (a loadable module) for Lua 5.4, LuaJIT or LuaRocks. There are 26 examples and every BUI widget type works. Vue and Angular would be thin adapters over @blender-ui/native , the layer React and Svelte already share ( how to add a framework ). Ruby and Go (through cgo) would call the C kit, BUI_kit.h . If you want one sooner, open an issue or a pull request: CONTRIBUTING.md says how. Is it ready for production? Much of it is complete and tested (the C kit, tkinter, the components, Rust, Dear ImGui, JavaScript), and some parts are partial or experimental (Qt syntax, parts of CSS and text, macOS). Status and roadmap shows which is which. Pin your version, and test on the platforms you ship. Who wrote it? LLMs. Not in the way you think. Instead of porting it, we asked an LLM to remove everything that isn't UI logic, and then ported the drawing and interaction code from Blender's sources. Turns out LLMs are better at removing than at generating. We call it Vibe-Pruning. Why GPL? BUI is derived from Blender's source code, so it follows Blender's licensing: the whole is under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later, and individual files keep their own compatible license (`GPL-2.0-or-later` for the files that come from Blender). Is it immediate mode? Is there a visual UI editor? BUI is retained-mode: it keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI, and redraws only what changed. There is no visual UI editor yet; you write the UI in code (tkinter, Qt-style, Blender components, Rust, JavaScript or C). Is the C API stable? Not before 1.0, but it is versioned: BUI_kit.h has BUI_KIT_VERSION_* macros and BK_version() reports the library's version, the same number as the Python, Rust and npm packages. Every change that breaks existing code is listed under "C API changes" in the changelog. Pin a release number, not a commit. From 1.0 it follows semantic versioning ( details ). Is BUI accessible to screen readers? Not yet. See the known limitations . Can I use BUI in a commercial app? The GPL allows commercial use. What it asks is that when you distribute a program that includes BUI, you distribute it under the GPL too, with its source code available. If that doesn't fit your project, talk to a lawyer before you ship. (This is a summary, not legal advice.) Star History 43. Contributing and publishing Contributions are welcome: bug reports, missing tkinter/Qt behavior, CSS features, platform hosts and docs. If you have a Mac, running the Cocoa host and reporting what happens is one of the most useful things you can do right now. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, and please follow the Code of Conduct . Report security issues privately, as SECURITY.md describes. Releases go to PyPI ( blenderui , wheels built by CI on a v* tag), crates.io (the eight Rust crates, in dependency order) and npm ( @blender-ui/native , @blender-ui/react ). The steps are in docs/publishing.md . 44. License and credits License. BUI follows Blender's licensing. BUI as a whole is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (the text is in LICENSE ). Individual files may have a different, but compatible license: the files that come from Blender keep Blender's SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header, and new files carry the same one. Third-party parts keep their own licenses: Part What it does in BUI License Blender sources Widget drawing, interaction rules, theme, icons, blenlib , GHOST window code, the File Browser and node editor GPL-2.0-or-later Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut The immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI MIT Inter by Rasmus Andersson The embedded UI font, as in Blender ( gpu/extern/Inter-LICENSE.txt ) SIL Open Font License 1.1 FreeType 2.13.3 Glyph loading, hinting and rendering, like Blender's BLF FreeType License or GPLv2 (dual-licensed) stb_truetype by Sean Barrett Font metrics and character maps, and the fallback rasterizer Public domain NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen, as edited by Blender Rasterizing Blender's SVG icons Zlib Wuffs by Google Decoding PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA and QOI images MIT or Apache-2.0 (used as MIT) libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 Decoding JPEG images IJG, BSD-3-Clause and zlib libwebp 1.6.0 Decoding WebP images, including animation BSD-3-Clause Slug by Eric Lengyel The GPU glyph coverage algorithm (shader code "Copyright 2017 by Eric Lengyel") MIT Tailwind CSS The v4 default theme values behind the Tailwind support MIT The Rust and JavaScript bindings also depend on crates and packages such as taffy, napi-rs, React and QuickJS, each under its own license. The full license texts of everything above, and of every Rust crate BUI's packages are built from, are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . It ships inside the Python wheels, the npm packages and the crates, and python tools/gen_notices.py regenerates it. Acknowledgments. Thank you to: Blender and its community: the UI this project is built from, including its GHOST window code and blenlib. Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut: the immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI. taffy : flexbox, grid and block layout for the Rust crate. Tailwind CSS : the v4 theme behind the Tailwind support. FreeType : glyph rendering, as in Blender. stb_truetype : font metrics and the fallback rasterizer. NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen: the icon rasterizer, via Blender's edited copy. Inter by Rasmus Andersson: the embedded UI font, as in Blender. Slug by Eric Lengyel: the GPU glyph coverage algorithm. gpui , zopra and Leptos : the APIs the Rust syntax follows. BUI is Blender's UI, minus the default cube. You're free to add your own. About Blender's GPU Accelerated UI, Decoupled from it's original codebase. Supports Rust, Python, JS, Lua, C & C++. title: Pwn.college
body_text: pwn.college pwn . college Dojos Workspace Help Chat Search Register Login Hide Navbar pwn . college Learn to Hack! You have entered the pwn.college DOJO, an education platform for learners to develop and practice core cybersecurity skills in a hands-on fashion. Entering, you receive your "white belt" , signifying the beginning of your hacker life. From here, you will learn cybersecurity by diving deep into the core of computing, using that journey to absorb cybersecurity concepts. This will involve melding your mind to your terminal, whispering instructions to the CPU, and strumming bits directly onto networks. That terminal cursor blinking above? It will be your stalwart companion through this adventure as you practice, earn your belts , and, eventually, make perfect. Every dojo has its sensei. This platform is maintained by an awesome team of hackers at Arizona State University. It powers much of ASU's cybersecurity curriculum, and is open, for free, to participation for interested people around the world! Enjoy your journey! If you have questions, comments, suggestions, and feedback, please join our Discord server or email us at [email protected] ! The Rules The challenges created for pwn.college are, first and foremost, educational material, and are used to grade students at universities around the world. Because of this, we would appreciate that you do not post writeups, walkthrough videos, and livestreams of challenge solutions to the internet. Obviously, we can't enforce this, but we worked hard to make all of this public, and we would appreciate your help in keeping pwn.college a viable educational platform. Please agree to these rules to continue to the material! I Agree to the Rules YOUR Journey — Next Steps 🫵 Whether you have just started, or have come far, there is always a next step to your journey. The dojo or dojos listed below is that step, presented to you in the order that you should learn them . Take a step, and the next will reveal itself. Start Here 63 Hacking 2 Modules 10 Challenges Side Quests Want to work ahead? Know your path better than we do? Forge your path through our whole material ! Need a break? Want to learn something new? Check out dojos created by the pwn.college community! Sharing is Caring Want to use pwn.college in your course? No problem! You can use the videos and slides of pwn.college lectures freely for non-commercial purposes, but please provide attribution! Additionally, if you use pwn.college in your own education program, we would appreciate it if you email us to let us know. Evidence of wide-spread use of pwn.college for education will be a huge help for our various academic careers! EDUCATORS: If you are an educational institution and are using pwn.college as part of a class, you can import our challenges (or add your own) into your own private dojo for your students! Create your dojo here . CONFERENCES: If you are running a conference and would like pwn.college presence there (as a form of intense weekend-long training), please email us! After pwn.college Eventually, hackers continue their journey beyond pwn.college, becoming certain in their skills, achieving brown belt status (and able to, for example, usefully contribute to the cybersecurity industry and academia), before finally graduating to hacking masters: black belts . But this, unfortunately, must happen outside of the dojo (for now!). Some suggestions: Capture The Flags (CTFs) are a great way to practice your hacking skills in a fun and ethical way. The most popular way to find upcoming events is at https://ctftime.org . There is also a list of introductory CTFs here . If you are at ASU, feel free to check out and join ASU’s enigmatic hacking club . Wargames are another great way to practice your hacking skills. Whereas CTFs are short (normally 48 hour) events, wargames are not time-based. You can find a list of wargames at https://github.com/zardus/wargame-nexus . There are many other awesome learning platforms, such as CryptoHack and OST2 that will help teach you explore new topics! If you want to get involved with cybersecurity research, but don’t know how, consider joining us for an internship at ASU . Contributing The infrastructure powering pwn.college is open source, and we welcome pull requests and issues. Some of the modules are closed-source, because they include source code and solution scripts, but others can be found on github . If you are an educator, or otherwise someone we trust, and are interested in collaborating on the modules themselves, please email us at [email protected] . Likewise, drop us a line if you are interested in collaborating on the slides! Resource Index We use a lot of different resources and platforms. Here they are! Lectures on YouTube Live Broadcasts on Twitch Chat on Discord Open Source on GitHub Contact us via Email Powered by pwn.college Interested in dedicated training or tailored services for your organization? Find out more .

Voor online betalingsverkeer via het nieuwe iDEAL | Wero gelden vanuit Europese wetgeving strenge regels rondom privacy, veiligheid en het voorkomen van fraude. iDEAL | Wero stelt daarom hoge eisen aan de beveiliging en integriteit van apparaten die gebruik maken van de betaalmethode. iDEAL | Wero maakt gebruik van de standaard beveiligingscontroles voor reguliere besturingssystemen. Doordat alternatieve systemen deze ingebouwde beveiligingen overslaan of vervangen, garandeert iDEAL | Wero de veiligheid van de transactie niet. Als bank maken we voor onze dienstverlening regelmatig gebruik van externe leveranciers. Waar mogelijk beoordelen we de risico's op het gebied van privacy, informatiebeveiliging en continuïteit, en proberen we deze te beperken tot een acceptabel niveau. Zijn de risico's onacceptabel, dan maken we geen gebruik van de leverancier. Voor gezamenlijke betaalinitiatieven, zoals iDEAL | Wero, volgen we de kaders en veiligheidseisen die partijen gezamenlijk vaststellen. De mogelijkheden voor de toekomst We onderzoeken met iDEAL | Wero of alternatieve besturingssystemen in de toekomst worden ondersteund. Dat hangt af van meerdere partijen en technologische ontwikkelingen. Daarover kunnen we op dit moment niets toezeggen of garanderen. Conclusie ASN Bank werkt met Nederlandse en Europese partijen aan de verdere ontwikkeling en beschikbaarheid van iDEAL | Wero. Op dit moment ondersteunen we de dienst nog niet op alle toestellen en besturingssystemen. Daarom bieden we u helaas geen oplossing waarmee u iDEAL | Wero alsnog op uw telefoon gebruikt. I think Fairphone selling phones with Android or /e/OS preinstalled is a stronger argument against strong integrity. Motorola probably won't sell phones with Graphene preinstalled, but the Graphene being 'supported' on Motorola phones might help with legitimising it as far as ASN is concerned. ThijsRay commented on Nov 7, 2026 ThijsRay on Nov 7, 2026 More actions Honestly, I find this ridiculous. I understand that they just try to implement the Wero specification, but why is this a requirement? Why do we need Google's blessing to use a supposedly independent European payment system? This requirement does not exist within Wero. Perhaps requirement is not the right word then. I wrote this based on the reply from ASN and this reply from EPI/Wero, shared earlier in this thread, emphasis mine: EPI Central Services and our underlying payment tokenisation components require assurance on several layers before issuing tokens with payment authority : that the application binary has not been tampered with or repackaged, that the app is distributed through an authentic channel, and that the operating system has not been modified or hooked by debugging or emulation tools. Google Play Integrity provides these combined signals in a signed token that our backend verifies server-to-server. Hardware key attestation is an important building block, but on its own it does not give the full application and OS integrity verification that our risk and fraud models require. I understand that some form of integrity is required. But EPI/Wero currently assumes that Google Play Integrity is the only method of validating the integrity of the execution environment. As other in this thread have pointed out, that is not the case. Google Play Integrity is not the only method. The standard Android hardware attestation API CAN be just as well be used to verify the authenticity/integrity of the hardware, firmware, OS and the app running on top of it. If Google Play Integrity is the only method allowed or supported by EPI, then your phone has to be blessed/verified by Google before you can use Wero. To me, it seems silly to have such a strong dependency on Google for a European payment system. Perhaps not all banks implement the integrity check using Google Play Integrity as EPI recommends right now, perhaps some banks already use hardware key attestation. Great! But that should be something that is officially supported by EPI as well to prevent situations like we have now with the ASN bank app. 👍 React with 👍 3 Reacted by Stephan Paternotte, anna-or-rey and Cosmin Polifronie Stephan-P commented on Nov 8, 2026 Stephan-P on Nov 8, 2026 More actions And still results can be mixed, as yesterday I had no trouble fulfilling a €800 Wero/Ideal (?) payment using the ASN app. My Pixel 7a: GOS 2026110201 Google Play Store Google play services ASN Bank app 1.36.4 Stephan-P commented on Nov 8, 2026 Stephan-P on Nov 8, 2026 More actions Would it be an idea to craft a boilerplate call, template if you will, towards banks and payment services, including all the valid arguments towards adding the standard AOSP device integrity authentication, so that safe and secure Android devices, such as GrapheneOS can be supported? Any user could take this boilerplate to inform their bank or payment service provider about their issues with the current state of affairs and request due support of their digital device. lucasvbeek commented on Nov 8, 2026 lucasvbeek on Nov 8, 2026 More actions And still results can be mixed, as yesterday I had no trouble fulfilling a €800 Wero/Ideal (?) payment using the ASN app. 'Wero | iDeal' is just iDeal with updated branding. Some payments are now starting to use 'Wero', which uses different tech and is blocked on GOS. thestinger commented on Nov 8, 2026 thestinger on Nov 8, 2026 More actions They're incorrect about what the Android key attestation API provides. It includes support for verifying the hardware, firmware, OS and app are genuine. It provides a signed result with the verified boot state, verified boot key fingerprint, major OS version and OS patch levels. It also includes the app package name, version code and signing key fingerprints. The key attestation API is what the Play Integrity API itself uses for the strong integrity them. They're completely wrong about what it provides. You should explain this and link to https://grapheneos.org/articles/attestation-compatibility-guide . 👍 React with 👍 4 Reacted by Orazio, Wouter, Daniël de Kok and fckff thestinger commented on Nov 8, 2026 thestinger on Nov 8, 2026 More actions We need our users to start pushing back against these kinds of false claims and linking to https://grapheneos.org/articles/attestation-compatibility-guide . Please contact your national and EU political representatives about this. The EU should not be participating in locking out anything not approved by Apple or Google for completely illegitimate reasons. App developers and governments are being misled by Google. Play Integrity API is not a security feature and does not enforce any serious security checks or standards. It exists to enforce the highly anti-competitive Google Mobile Services licensing model to protect and expand Google's monopolies. By implementing any requirement for it, they're heavily assisting with wiping out any chance of serious competition with Google Mobile Services and Apple devices in the future. 👍 React with 👍 2 Reacted by Daniël de Kok and fckff noughtmare commented on Nov 8, 2026 noughtmare on Nov 8, 2026 More actions Please contact your national and EU political representatives about this. The EU should not be participating in locking out anything not approved by Apple or Google for completely illegitimate reasons. Note that Wero is a private initiative by European banks (EPI), so I don't think EU representatives have much influence on this besides not making the same mistake with their upcoming “digital euro” which hopefully will become a Wero competitor. title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
body_text: x This website requires javascript to properly function. Consider activating javascript to get access to all site functionality. LESSWRONG LW Login Arjun Panickssery's Shortform — LessWrong Arjun Panickssery's Shortform by Arjun Panickssery 30th Dec 2023 1 min read 136 5 This is a special post for quick takes by Arjun Panickssery . Only they can create top-level comments. Comments here also appear on the Quick Takes page and All Posts page . Rendering 0 / 136 comments, sorted by top scoring (show all) Click to highlight new comments since: Today at 2:11 AM Moderation Log More from Arjun Panickssery View more Curated and popular this week 136 Comments 136 Comment Permalink Arjun Panickssery 3d * 134 69 I struggle to believe at an intuitive level that autonomous R&D is so ingenious. I have been monitoring a few side projects: Building a new SOTA engine for Scrabble (current SOTA is not really a neural-network method and doesn't beat the strongest human player) Building a bot to play Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe Researching philosophy and formalizing some proofs for the AI Philosophy contest In all of these cases, the model's judgment is just very poor in a basic way. For example: When reviewing literature, it fails to identify the specific papers or blog posts that are obviously the most important and useful. It will conduct experiments that have no information value because the amount of training data used was obviously too small to distinguish the architectures to be compared. In the philosophy project, where it built a wiki over many tokens and investigations, it kept going down directions which were extremely trivial and had little value. For Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, I saw a very clever idea in a blog post that I doubt Astra would ever have come up with; it actually located the blog post but didn't realize its importance or relevance (which could be discerned easily from his strong performance in an online arena and the recency of the post) over papers from previous years that are obviously less relevant. I judged an Apart hackathon last weekend and reviewed eight papers, all of which scored between 60% and 95% on Pangram. Predictably, the papers were often very similar to each other, and kind of methodologically incomplete in a vague but similar way, where they seem to overlook the most straightforward analysis. Maybe the important exception is certain hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops. For example, I improved the SOTA on "listing all legal Scrabble moves" by 10x just by prompting Astra over and over to try harder, to aim for <specific performance level>, to "systematically try every method in the literature that seems kind of related," etc. But even in that case, two big leaps were when I said that it should take into account the fact that you can measure across a game rather than per random position, and suggesting that it try to design algorithms for three different cases based on the number of blank tiles left in the bag (which cause the number of moves to explode). There is also the fact that Astra at least (and presumably Claude) tends to write reports that are extremely difficult to understand and some kind of Q&A interrogation is often needed to figure out what it actually did and what the key results are. Maybe there's a temptation to just say "whatever" and let it rip. Reply Showing 3 of 14 replies (Click to show all) -1 T431 2d Monitoring AI game performance in these times must be interesting. A few years ago, I was monitoring AI skill in Hanabi but dropped it after DeepMind archived their environment repository for it; I am not sure where things stand w/ AI in Hanabi but it may be another avenue for you to examine. @GPT6 Astra What is the current state of AI research in the game of Hanabi? ChatGPT Astra 2d 3 0 Still active—the repository’s archival didn’t end the research. The key distinction is self-play versus cooperation with unfamiliar partners. Specialist self-play: Ataraxos (September 2026), using reinforcement learning plus search, reports averages of 24.65/25 with two players, 24.86 with three, and 24.41 with five. Generalization: R3D2 (ICLR 2025) handles different player counts and unfamiliar partners. The Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge benchmarks cooperation with human-like partners; high self-play scores don’t guarantee this. LLMs: An ICML 2026 study found its strongest tested models scoring roughly 15–18/25, despite prompting and deduction scaffolds—well below specialist agents. Importantly, these were mostly 2025-generation models, including o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, not a measurement of today’s frontier. So Hanabi remains useful for studying coordination, rather than merely maximizing scores with copies of oneself. Reply View run 5 DirectedEvolution 2d I’ve been rewriting python functions to strip out variable names, comments, etc. and testing model abilities to determine what mathematical method the function implements. While increasing model size through Claude Opus 5.5 does improve success, there are many problems on which they consistently fail to recognize solutions unless supplied with a sufficient hint, even if provided with the results of automated test inputs. I want to flag that I don’t currently have a reproducible benchmark. There are just informal results I’ve obtained in the process of working on a codebase inspection tool. These and related results suggest to me that even advanced models continue to rely on name-matching to deliver low cost, reliable answers for many problems. Clearly, that’s nevertheless compatible with producing Fields-medal-quality mathematical proofs. See in context

title: Greece has its own Pompeii: Thera buried Akrotiri in ash 17th-16th century BCE
body_text: Bronze Age Akrotiri Is Greek's Pompeii Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. History | November 3, 2026 Greece Has Its Own Pompeii, and the Ruins Tell a Captivating Story of a Sophisticated, Seafaring Bronze Age Society The Thera volcano, on modern-day Santorini, buried Akrotiri in ash in the 17th or 16th century B.C.E. The eruption was one of the largest in recorded history The ruins of Akrotiri, a Bronze Age settlement on what is now the Greek island of Santorini Westend61 via Getty Images Greece Has Its Own Pompeii, and the Ruins Tell a Captivating Story of a Sophisticated, Seafaring Bronze Age Society The Thera volcano, on modern-day Santorini, buried Akrotiri in ash in the 17th or 16th century B.C.E. The eruption was one of the largest in recorded history Aileen Weintraub | Freelance writer November 3, 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source The ruins of Akrotiri, a Bronze Age settlement on what is now the Greek island of Santorini Westend61 via Getty Images The earth rumbled for days. Inhabitants of the seafaring Bronze Age settlement of Akrotiri watched smoke plume from Thera , a long-dormant volcano on what is now the Greek island of Santorini . People gathered their belongings and safely stored the valuables they were forced to leave behind. Then they fled by boat to nearby islands. When these minor earthquakes and eruptions subsided, residents returned to Akrotiri, collecting materials for reconstruction and beginning the arduous process of repairing the damage . But the ground continued to tremble. As conditions worsened , they made the difficult decision to flee once more, hopeful that their homes would survive the coming devastation. When Thera erupted again, the explosion was so powerful that it destroyed Akrotiri, burying the settlement (and the island that shared the volcano’s name) in some 200 feet of ash and pumice stone. The timing of the disaster is the subject of intense debate , but scholars generally date it to between 1620 and 1530 B.C.E. The event was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recorded history: Thera released about four times more volcanic material than the infamous Krakatau eruption, which killed upwards of 36,000 people in what is now Indonesia in 1883. A 2000 satellite image of Santorini. The bay at the center of the island is the volcanic caldera created by Thera's eruption. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons The fallout of the Thera eruption The ash cloud formed by the Thera eruption completely transformed the island’s lush, humid environment into an arid one. Ash from the volcano was so widespread that it rained down as far as modern-day Egypt and Israel. Layers of sand and pebbles found between archaeological deposits suggest that multiple tsunamis also contributed to the destruction. But the biggest fallout of this cataclysmic event happened when a portion of the volcanic caldera collapsed into the sea a few days after the eruption, forever changing the landscape of Santorini. This plummet into the depths of the Aegean Sea has become the stuff of legends . Some claim that Akrotiri is the lost city of Atlantis , which the Greek philosopher Plato described centuries later, around 360 B.C.E. Most modern scholars, however, agree that Plato created the tale of the sunken island as an allegorical device. Did you know? The legend of Atlantis In Plato’s telling, Atlantis was home to descendants of the sea god Poseidon , who turned on his progeny after they proved unworthy of his favor. According to the London-based Horniman Museum & Gardens , “The tale warns against the dangers of power and corruption, as well as stressing the importance of goodness.” Plato’s Timaeus suggests that Atlantis succumbed to “violent earthquakes and floods, and in a single day of misfortune,” the island “disappeared in the depths of the sea.” Much like the Roman city of Pompeii , which was destroyed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E. , Akrotiri was preserved beneath the ash. “Everything was absolutely annihilated and completely encapsulated on the island,” says Lefteris Zorzos , an archaeologist whose research focuses on the prehistoric landscape of Santorini. This created a rare time capsule that provides an unprecedented look into the daily life of this Middle Bronze Age Cycladic civilization , so called after the Aegean islands where the culture flourished between about 3000 and 1000 B.C.E. Santorini remained uninhabited for some 700 years . According to the ancient Greek historian Herodotus , Phoenicians started repopulating the island in the ninth century B.C.E. But more than 2,500 years would pass before archaeologists uncovered the ruins of ancient Akrotiri beneath the layers of dirt and ash. Discovering Akrotiri In 1866, miners working in pumice quarries on the island of Therasia , directly west of Thera, discovered a prehistoric building while collecting ash to insulate the Suez Canal . The French School at Athens launched a small excavation of the area in 1870, but a large-scale dig at Akrotiri only commenced nearly a century later, in 1967 , under the leadership of archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos . A map of Bronze Age Thera, the Cyclades, Crete and the Peloponnese / Illustration by Meilan Solly Marinatos had previously studied the excavated ruins of the Minoan Palace of Knossos in Crete, tracing pumice found on the island, some 74 miles south of Santorini, to the Thera eruption. His research marked the first time that the destruction of Akrotiri was directly linked to the decline of the Minoans , who are often identified as Europe’s first advanced civilization. Marinatos posited that the earthquakes from Thera were so widespread, they toppled buildings and palaces on Crete. He also suggested that the resulting tsunamis damaged Minoan coastal settlements and halted shipping trade. But this theory is no longer widely accepted, and many historians now believe that the Minoans’ decline can’t be attributed to a single factor . Instead, they point to a combination of environmental changes, declining trade, political instability and conflicts with the ascendant Mycenean civilization . Preserving an ancient site that was found remarkably intact presented a unique challenge for Marinatos. “When you excavate, you’re destroying a layer, removing the earth that’s keeping it all together,” Zorzos says. “You have to deal with this differently than you would a site that’s not as well preserved.” Before Marinatos could proceed, he had to build a shelter atop the ruins so they wouldn’t crumble when exposed to the elements. Archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos photographs objects excavated on the island of Santorini, circa 1970 ullstein bild via Getty Images Under the leadership of Marinatos and his successor, Christos Doumas , archaeologists have excavated sites across Akrotiri down to the bedrock, allowing scientists to study the island’s stratigraphy as far back as 6,500 years ago. Zorzos estimates that the ongoing excavations have uncovered only about 10 percent of the settlement. The rest is still preserved beneath layers of ash and sediment. Surprisingly, researchers have yet to recover the remains of any Akrotiri residents killed by the eruption, suggesting that the majority, if not all, of the settlement’s inhabitants made it out alive after receiving warning of the impending disaster. (Excavations in Turkey have, however, revealed the skeletons of a teenager and a dog believed to be victims of a post-eruption tsunami, testifying to the event’s far reach.) Comparatively, archaeologists excavating the ruins of Pompeii continue to find victims’ skeletons (or the cavities left behind by bodies trapped in volcanic ash) nearly 2,000 years after Vesuvius’ eruption. Researchers can easily understand why Akrotiri’s inhabitants chose to settle in this area. “It has visibility and access to Crete, and it’s strategically connected to the rest of the Cycladic Islands,” says Marianna Nikolaidou , an archaeologist specializing in Aegean culture at the University of California, Los Angeles. View of ruins at the Akrotiri archaeological site Public domain via Wikimedia Commons Akrotiri’s location at the crossroads of North Africa, Europe and the Middle East allowed for substantial maritime trade during the Early Bronze Age (circa 3000 to 2000 B.C.E.). Archaeological evidence suggests that the island community included farmers, fishers and craftspeople. By the Middle Bronze Age, Crete’s thriving Minoan civilization had left its mark on Akrotiri. The Minoans shared major advancements in architecture with their neighbors, encouraging them to construct multistory buildings adorned with detailed frescoes, paved streets and an impressive drainage system that included indoor plumbing. In total, archaeologists have identified and researched 35 buildings across Akrotiri. The settlement’s ancient residents “didn’t have access to forests or concrete, and still they are building three- and four-story-high buildings using limited wood, volcanic stones, mud and vegetation,” Zorzos says. “It’s phenomenal to think of how much they were able to achieve without access to modern tools.” 5 Surprising Facts About Pompeii Watch on The art and artifacts of Akrotiri Frescoes in excellent condition adorn the walls of many homes and public buildings in Akrotiri. “Every house had a fresco with a distinct ritual characteristic, and many of them are female-centered,” Nikolaidou says. Xeste 3 , a multistory structure with 14 rooms on each floor, boasts two well-preserved wall paintings. Nikolaidou praises the frescoes’ treatment of their chosen themes, as well as the preparation and finish of the plaster on which they were painted. The first scene depicts three women in a field with crocus flowers and an altar, while the second portrays a different group of women collecting crocuses , which they offer to a goddess attended by a blue monkey and a griffin. The crocus was a significant symbol in antiquity, with the plant used as a spice, perfume, dye or medicine. “On an island like this with limited resources, crocus must have been a source of economic prosperity, and the fact that it’s associated with women hints to the participation of women in agricultural production and the economic aspects of life, not just the ritual aspects,” Nikolaidou says. This Akrotiri fresco shows women gathering saffron crocus. Holger Uwe Schmitt via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0 In addition to well-preserved architecture and art, excavations at Akrotiri have unearthed vessels and beads from necklaces. Not much jewelry has been uncovered because inhabitants typically took such valuables with them when they fled. Many of the ceramics depict scenes similar to the wall paintings, providing important clues regarding daily life on the island. Vessels used for transporting oil and wine, and for storing food, feature polychrome scenes of swallows, dolphins and crocuses . Charred remains of barley and fava beans found on the bottom of some of the jugs provide a rare look at the early Mediterranean diet. One of the most interesting pottery shapes identified at the site is the nippled ewer . “These jugs have a bulbous body, with little pinches that are painted to imitate nipples,” Nikolaidou says. Some of the vessels are even adorned with earrings and necklaces, underscoring the jug’s symbolism as a representation of the female body. The preservation and future of Akrotiri Marinatos died in 1974, after an onsite fall during excavations at Akrotiri. Doumas replaced him as director of the archaeological project and has held the position ever since. In 2012, he oversaw the installation of a bioclimatic shelter designed to help preserve the site . The three-acre shelter protects the fragile buildings, with discreet fans extracting the hot air from the surrounding environment. The structure also offers visitors relief from the Mediterranean sun while they explore this settlement frozen in time. An Akrotiri fresco of a ship procession Holger Uwe Schmitt via Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0 The Akrotiri archaeological site is open to the public most days of the week. Visitors are welcome to explore on their own or with a tour guide who can provide an in-depth explanation of each structure. The nearby Museum of Prehistoric Thera , located about 20 minutes away by car, houses many of the site’s artifacts and is worth a visit. More than three and a half millennia after Thera’s eruption, the Santorini community is working with the Archaeological Society at Athens to continue to preserve and fund the site. In 2027, Santorini will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the official start of excavations—an occasion that will be marked with exhibitions, educational programs and other events. Akrotiri’s ruins have revealed the long-overlooked story of a cosmopolitan society connected to the outside world. The settlement’s inhabitants were voyagers and artisans with sophisticated and clearly defined social stratification, but they also had a strong sense of collectivity and community that survives on Santorini today. “It’s one of the most important archaeological sites in the world,” Zorzos says. “It provides a window into life in the prehistoric Aegean like we’ve never seen before.” You Might Also Like First Human Skeleton From Bronze Age Tsunami Discovered in Turkey January 5, 2022 A Remarkable Fresco Depicting a Scene From Greek Mythology Has Been Found in Pompeii March 5, 2024 Who Were the Painters of Pompeii? CREATE AN ACCOUNT SIGN IN Computing News The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt Dina Genkina 02 Nov 2026 4 min read Dina Genkina is the computing and hardware editor at IEEE Spectrum iStock In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server. As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI. “One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.” PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed. “If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University . “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately. Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.” AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible. “There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.” This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models . “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.” Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.” Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green , an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.” In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.” One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.” From Your Site Articles Your AI Agent Is Now a Target for Email Phishing › With $1 Cyberattacks on the Rise, Durable Defenses Pay Off › What Anthropic’s Mythos Means for the Future of Cybersecurity › Related Articles Around the Web The PHP Foundation — The PHP Foundation — Supporting, Advancing, and Developing the PHP Language › cybersecurity internet artificial intelligence Dina Genkina Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. She holds a PhD in atomic physics and lives in Brooklyn. title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
body_text: PhobosLab Blog Games Projects Dominic Szablewski, @phoboslab — Tuesday, November 3rd 2026 Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64 Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time. But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited. Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it. Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer. This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB. So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question. Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay. Audio in the Open Source Libdragon Similar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon , the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space. Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this “obsolete” hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay. What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse. QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize. A simple transform codec, something like MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work… The Ultra Low Complexity Codec During some late-night “research” , I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare. ulcplayer-gba by Aikku93, recorded in a Game Boy Advance emulator Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU . For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill. So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC). ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax. In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it. The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change: -7 … -2 , 2 … 7 - coefficient value 0 - zero run, run length ( 1 … 16 ) follows in the next nibble 1 - long zero run, run length ( 17 … 288 ) follows in the next two nibbles -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C . Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is . ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications. Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then! ULC on the N64 I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch. The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU. Float to 16-bit Fixed Point Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer. That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point. While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving at 3072 bytes : 32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14). After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is. Cramming it into the RSP Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor. This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job. (Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now) So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL . Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer. The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP. The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all. My ulc64 demo demonstrating quality at various bitrates To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio. ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects. The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago. Addendum A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. The README states: [...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image. ~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos! © 2026 Dominic Szablewski – Imprint – powered by Pagenode (4ms) – made with <3

title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
body_text: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS - Karthikey Hegde / karthihegde / contact / posts So my ISP was hijacking my DNS Published on November 3, 2026 It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working. I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address. "Huh?" was my exact reaction. I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address. Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up . But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one. So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way. I self host Unbound I am safe For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver. Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic. But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit. Just use DNSSEC It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption. You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses. And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , only 7.03% of graded domains have a valid, fully validating DNSSEC chain. If a tampered response fails DNSSEC validation, your resolver will return SERVFAIL instead of handing you that bogus IP address. DoH and DoT are not Tamper free And yes, this is true. DoT and DoH rely on you trusting the DNS resolver you're sending your queries to. They encrypt the connection, so your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS traffic in transit. But that doesn't mean the resolver itself can't mess with your responses. You're still putting your trust in whoever runs that DNS server. Your ISP can snoop on the sites regardless Indeed. Although your regular internet traffic is encrypted with TLS, your ISP can see the hostname during the TLS handshake (SNI). They can also figure out which site you're visiting just from the destination IP sometimes. Unless, of course, you tunnel your traffic through a VPN. I use Mullvad through Tailscale's exit node feature. Of course, this just shifts some of the trust to your VPN provider. But that's a story for another day. So what does my setup look like? I've been using Pi-hole/AdGuard for over 3 years now. That's actually what got me into self-hosting in the first place. But there's another reason I don't route every single container through my local DNS server. When I'm updating containers, if something goes wrong and my DNS server goes down, I don't want that to take down DNS resolution for other containers that depend on it. So for some containers, I wanted an external DNS resolver as a fallback. Right now, I use AdGuard for my DNS, with dnscrypt-proxy handling the upstream DNS queries over DNSCrypt, so my DNS traffic is encrypted in transit. For containers where I really can't afford DNS failures, I also have Cloudflare configured as a fallback. My local AdGuard is still the primary DNS for them, though. I also run NixOS on my servers, and my dotfiles are open source if you're interested

body_text: MCP Explained Â· how the Model Context Protocol works MCP Explained What is MCP? by Model Context Protocol What is MCP? An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back. Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope.
